speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were all profoundly shocked when we learned early yesterday afternoon of the terrible aircraft accident at Moose Jaw which snuffed out instantaneously the lives of the thirty-one passengers of the T.C.A. air liner, of the four members of its crew, of the pilot of the R.C.A.F. trainer craft involved with the liner in a mid-air collision, and of one more person on the ground suffocated in the ruins of a home destroyed by the flaming wreckage of the planes.
Our warmhearted sympathy reached out at once to all those so tragically bereaved.
But for each one of us in this house our grief became an even more personal thing when the liner's passenger list was made public and Mr. and Mrs. Adamson's names appeared in it. It is truly said that despite our differences in political outlook friendships are formed in this house without regard to party lines. No political difference ever stood in the way of becoming a friend of Rodney Adamson. Our colleague had qualities that endeared him to all of us. His unassuming manner was but one of the many aspects of his solicitude for his fellow men, and throughout his life he used his abilities to the full to work and to fight in their interests.
He was only thirteen years of age when the first world war broke out but somehow, despite his youth, he contrived to serve his country overseas as a pilot before the conflict was over. When the second world war broke out he might well have felt that he had already done his duty to his country in warfare, but his patriotism was such that he could not take any easy course. Once more he served overseas as an officer in the Lome Scots.
He was first elected to this house in 1940 for the Ontario constituency of York West and was returned by his constituents in each succeeding general election. With characteristic vigour he displayed his interest in a wide variety of the activities of parliament and was one of the official opposition's first-line debaters. Those of us who sit on this
side of Mr. Speaker, while not agreeing with all of the things he said, listened to him with respect, for we knew that when Mr. Adamson spoke he spoke after careful preparation and with strong conviction.
He will be remembered in this chamber chiefly, I think, for his interest in conservation and in the development of our resources in the best interests of all Canadians. It will be recalled that during this session he emphasized, and it needed emphasis, the importance of our great northern region. The loss of our colleague and his devoted wife is a real one, and our heartfelt sympathy is extended to their children and their families. It is also extended, Mr. Speaker, to you personally and by all of us on this side of the house, to the Leader of the Opposition and the members of his party both in the house and in the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the members of families of both Mr. and Mrs. Adamson will appreciate the words of sympathy that have been expressed by the Prime Minister on behalf of all of us. It is always a tragic thing to realize that those with whom we have been so closely associated day by day have suddenly been taken from us, but there does seem to be a particularly tragic aspect to this accident when we realize that both of them, Rodney and Cynthia as we knew them, were with us only a few days ago, gay, vigorous and so friendly to everyone they met. As the Prime Minister has said, friendships are not in any way limited to the parties with which we are associated, and I know that there was warm and affectionate friendship for both of them in every part of this house.
Rodney Adamson came of a military family. In the first world war his father had commanded that very famous regiment, the Princess Patricia's. The son, both in the first war and the last war, served his country well. He continued his military interests.
As has already been pointed out in the press, Rodney Adamson went to some pains to keep himself informed. At some considerable risk he and his wife spent some time beyond the iron curtain seeking to learn something of what was taking place there. He served his own constituency and his country well. For fourteen years he has represented a large and very important part

The late Rodney Adamson of Ontario. We remember him best for his constant and unfailing interest in the conservation of resources, particularly the mining resources of this country. He was an advocate of free gold, and will always be remembered as one of those who had deep and strong convictions concerning the importance of gold in supporting the economy of our country.
At a time when there may be too great a tendency towards conformity, Rodney Adamson was an individualist. He never hesitated to express his own views with clarity and firmness, whether or not they happened to be the views that were generally accepted. He was the chairman of the committee of our party on natural resources, and we relied greatly on him and his knowledge of that subject. His wife was keenly interested in public affairs, and also served in uniform with distinction during the last war, when she commanded the Canadian women's army corps in Italy. She knew Europe well. She followed both domestic and international affairs, and the two of them were a very effective team in all that they were doing here in Ottawa. Of both of them, I think it could be appropriately said that they died on active service.
What happened in this case does emphasize the fact that all the members of this house are called upon to accept certain responsibilities which impose inescapable risks. Last night he was to have spoken in Calgary at a political meeting. This afternoon he was to have attended a reception specially arranged for him by his father's old regiment, the Princess Patricia's, in Calgary. This evening he was to have addressed that very famous organization, the United Services Club of Calgary. His public service activities were continued right to the end.
In speaking of him in this way and of the services that he performed, may I mention the fact that we had a very clear expression of the extent to which party lines leave no divisions at a time like this. I do want to say that no one could have been more thoughtful than was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in his attention to all the details connected with this very tragic event. I think it would be appropriate that I should also say that I do realize that this has been a great blow to him. Whatever differences of opinion there may have been at any time in regard to the details of administration or otherwise, I am sure there is no one in this house who has ever questioned the deep and abiding devotion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to that service with which he has been so closely


associated. The safety record of Trans-Canada Air Lines has been one of which all Canadians can be proud.
It is an unhappy circumstance that we should now be expressing sympathy in the death of one of our own members and his wife on the occasion of the first fatal accident there has been in so many years. I know the sympathy of every member here will go out in full measure to the mother and father of Mrs. Adamson; to the brother of Mr. Adamson; and particularly to their sons, one of whom is only five years old. The thoughts of all of us will be with them not only now but in the years ahead. At the same time may I say that our sympathy is extended to the families of all those who died in this terrible disaster. All Canadians will be thinking of them in their sorrow.

When the first news of this unaccountable accident reached the house, Mr. Speaker, there was general consternation because of the loss of life involved. Then, too, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has said, because of the exceptionally fine record of Trans-Canada Air Lines there was a feeling of regret that this happening should have occurred yesterday. But when later in the afternoon we learned that one of our own members and his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Adamson, were passengers on the plane there was not only the general feeling to which I have already referred, but a feeling of deep regret and deep sorrow at the loss of one of our members for whom all of us had a very high regard.
Rodney Adamson came here in 1940. I remember well when he came. I recall that we thought of him as a very kindly, friendly, new colleague. Throughout the years he vindicated the feeling we had at the outset of his appearance here. It is indeed a tragedy that he should be taken from our midst at this time, and with him his very charming wife. They leave two children behind and, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, not only will they be in our minds today, but I am sure that many of us will think of them throughout the days to come.
I should like to say, too, that we join with everyone in this house not only in expressing sympathy to the father and mother of Mrs. Adamson, to Mr. Adamson's brother, whom some of us know, and to the children, but to those bereaved friends and relatives of the others who died under these tragic circumstances. We think of the crew of the plane, because the crews of our Trans-Canada Air Lines are exceptionally careful-the splendid

record they have built up indicates that. We sympathize with them. We sympathize with the relatives of the passengers who were lost in this tragic occurrence.
As has been said here, when something of this sort strikes us, both as a House of Commons and as a country, I know that there is genuine sorrow for those who suffer under such tragic circumstances. We sympathize, too, with the friends and relatives of the woman on the ground who lost her life so suddenly when the flaming parts of the plane struck a home in the city of Moose Jaw. Perhaps later on, when an investigation has been made, it will be possible to say what error of judgment accounts for all this; and that brings to our minds that, after all, human judgment is often very unreliable. And so, on my colleagues' and my own behalf, I join with everyone in the house in expressing our sympathy to all who have been bereaved. I should like also to associate myself with the very genuine remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in regard to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who has shown such a keen interest in and is so justly proud of the great air line he has done so much to build.

Mr. Speaker, I am certain that the leader of this party would want me to express the feelings of our group. We join with others who have expressed sympathy on the sudden passing of Mr. Rodney Adamson and his wife. It brings to our minds once again the forcefulness of that truth, that we know not what a day may bring forth.
Mr. Adamson's office was in the same corridor as the offices of this group, and it meant that our paths very often met. At such times we had the opportunity to chat for a few moments with him. We felt he was a man who formed real convictions, and whose convictions really meant something to him. He will be missed by his party, because I am sure he was a most valuable asset to it. He will also be missed by the House of Commons and by his host of friends.
We join with others in offering our sympathy to those of his loved ones who are left to mourn his loss.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my words of tribute, because in doing so I feel I am voicing what is in the hearts of the people that Rodney Adamson represented in this Canadian parliament for so many years.
The late Rodney Adamson
The constituency of York-Humber was carved out of Mr. Adamson's constituency of York West. Some of the people for whom he spoke in this House of Commons are the people for whom I speak now. I know what a loss his death, and that of his wife Cynthia, will mean to those people, whom he served so faithfully.
The people of York West and of York-Humber were proud of Rodney Adamson, and they showed that pride by choosing him again and again from 1940, onward, to represent them in parliament. He had won their respect, their confidence and their affection as a public servant and as a man of the highest integrity. In York West and York-Humber we mourn the loss of a good friend and a good servant of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is reported today that Italy and Sweden have dropped out of the international wheat agreement, and that therefore they will not be taking up the amount of wheat they would have previously taken up-I believe the figure is 32 million bushels. Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce any comment to make on this information, in view of our present situation, and the accumulation of wheat that we have in this country?
3932	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the information I have is that Sweden has decided not to ratify. Sweden had a very small quota, indeed-a matter of two or three million bushels. That country has never been a considerable buyer of wheat. This year Sweden is actually an exporting country. It has exported seven or eight million bushels.
Italy did not ratify, owing to a change in government. Italy has still not ratified. Italy has applied to the council for a reduction in their quota. A meeting will be held to determine whether the reduction will be granted or not. I understand that if the reduction is granted Italy intends to sign. To date Italy has not ratified, but Italy has not indicated an intention of not ratifying.
Is there any possibility of other countries with commitments amounting to 32 million bushels, and that have not ratified the agreement, taking similar action?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Well, I have had no notice of these questions. The only country I recall that has not ratified is Brazil. Brazil indicated some time ago that they would not ratify the agreement, and Brazil had a considerable quota. However, Brazil is still buying wheat from North America, although they are buying outside the quota. The position is the same as that of the United Kingdom.
I think, aside from that, all the countries have ratified, except in the cases of Sweden and Italy.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the resolution passed by the legislature of Manitoba calling for amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which would enable farmers in Manitoba who suffered crop losses due to excessive moisture to receive further assistance? If so, is the minister prepared to recommend such amendments to parliament?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENTS REQUESTED BY MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank
the hon. member for having sent me a copy of his question. In view of the fact that it has come up on two or three occasions during this session, perhaps I should make a little longer statement than I made before with regard to it.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was passed in 1939 following seven years of drought on the prairies of western Canada, covering certain sections of the prairies. Because of the experience we had then, this house was persuaded to give consent to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The difficulties that have been experienced in Manitoba are not difficulties resulting from drought, but rather from excessive rainfall and excessive


moisture. These are difficulties which I think are prevalent right across Canada from time to time. I would think that if we were to make amendments such as those suggested in Manitoba they would have the effect in the first place of greatly increasing the payments that would have to be made not only in Manitoba, but from Manitoba through to the Rocky mountains.
Last year, as hon. members from the central part of the prairies know, there was a great deal of acreage, even on the heavy land surrounding Regina, that was without crops because they were not able to seed the land in the early part of the year. If we were to pass legislation of the kind which would meet conditions of that nature it would be most difficult to persuade the other parts of Canada to take the same action with regard to it as they took with regard to drought, which is of such a serious nature from time to time that it is almost impossible to provide any form of insurance that would take care of it, or to depend on any one province taking care of the calamity that comes when there is very widespread drought. For that reason I have written to the government of Manitoba, as a result of their having sent forward the resolution to me, and explained to them the reasons why I did not think it would be desirable to bring that proposed amendment into this house at this time, and I doubt very much whether it would be at any time unless we greatly change the policy which backs up the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

I have a few remarks I wish to make in connection with this department and the work they have on the agenda. I want to try to bring to the attention of the minister and his officials and of the members of the committee the need for more speed in connection with the trans-Canada highway. I also want to quote a few figures on the extent of the increase in traffic, motor vehicles and that sort of thing in Canada in the last few years, especially since 1949 when this project was first brought before parliament.
The Department of Public Works has announced that construction on the 5,000-mile trans-Canada highway was speeded up during 1953.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member please speak up so that we can hear him?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, if you could get some of the other members to pipe down, they might be able to hear me better.
Supply-Public Works
All provinces but Quebec have signed agreements with the federal government to share construction costs. The federal government pays half the cost of sections of previously-built roads incorporated in the trans-Canada highway. During 1953 contracts were approved worth $46,343,500, more than $12 million above the 1952 figure.
I wonder whether the hon. member would mind telling me what it is he is reading from?
I am reading from statistics from the Department of Public Works.
That is what I wanted to know. Is it a released statement?

It is a statement released by your department. That is the end of it.
At the end of the war economists felt that any prediction of 3 million vehicles in Canada by 1955 would be an overestimate. Already in 1952 we had reached that total. Now they are looking ahead to 1960 and later, and there is danger of being wrong as they were before. Some economists believe there will be 4,500,000 motor vehicles registered in Canada by 1960. I myself think the estimate is conservative. I believe we have 3,500,000 motor vehicles in Canada now. By the end of 1955 we will reach the 4 million mark. Add to this the influx of cars from the United States each year, and the congestion of traffic on our highways gives us some comprehension of the need of the trans-Canada highway now, not twenty years hence. At any rate our modern cars and trucks are in use to the point of embarrassment, and are getting more numerous all the time; and that is a challenge to this government in getting on with the job of this national project.
A study of the private services and of the public services rendered by the motor vehicle shows that a revolution has been brought about in our national transportation. A point has already been reached in use and ownership which leading authorities did not think we would attain for at least another ten years. The number of motor vehicles is ten years ahead of all predictions and traffic arteries are ten years behind.
In the annual use of their motor vehicles, Canadians now travel 12J billion miles per year. The tonnage of freight carried annually by motor transport in Canada exceeds the combined total of that carried by rail, water and air. There are 14,000 communities in this nation of ours which are chiefly dependent upon highway transportation for their very existence. If trucking were removed from industry for a brief period, the industrial machine would come to a halt in short order.

Supply-Public Works
Automotive vehicles play an indispensable role in the science of war and national defence. If we are to survive an attack on [DOT]our free world, we shall need all the mobility and powers of dispersal that automotive vehicles can give us, and most certainly a trans-Canada thoroughfare.
When confederation came into being it was quite properly believed that the railway would be the prime instrument of the country's development, that roads would be of limited local concern and should, therefore, be left entirely to the provinces to build and maintain. The fathers of confederation acted quite properly for their day and age. They were deliberating just about 35 years prior to the appearance of the first motor car in Canada. Hence roads have been principally the responsibility of municipal governments and the provinces. But the government of that day built two railroads across this continent. Without these rails of steel confederation would probably have fallen apart. It is just as important now to have a trans-Canada highway as it was to have a railroad at that time. These modern roads have become a matter of national importance. Most major traffic routes connect cities in different provinces and carry traffic to and from provinces. Eventually they will be largely interconnected in this national pattern of highways. But we are wondering: How soon? Roads are more than a provincial or municipal matter. They have become a national problem. We must have a broader area of co-operation and understanding among road-building authorities. Above all, we must have a stable and better highway policy, framed on national needs. It might be that some informal collaboration will result from the trans-Canada highway machinery. I, personally, believe that the best results will be achieved by a co-operative association of all road authorities in the interests of all. The problems that face us today dwarf the problems concerning roads of a generation ago. Every last citizen of Canada is or should be interested. The public does want this highway problem solved. People are ready to admit that they are learning by bitter experience, and that inadequate roads are a bad investment. They are paid for partly by human lives, by property damage and by costly delays. I am glad the Minister of Public Works inherited this problem from the last department in which he served, and I wish to quote a statement he made in 1949 when he was then minister of reconstruction and supply. He then moved the second reading of Bill No. 194 which was 
designed to encourage and assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway. On November 28, 1949, he said, as reported at page 2328 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in moving second reading of the bill entitled "An act to encourage and to assist in the construction of a trans-Canada highway." Hon. members will understand that this legislation is enabling in character, in that it seeks authority for the federal government to enter into agreements with the provincial governments toward the construction of provincial highways which will join at various provincial boundaries to form a continuous road across Canada from one coast to the other and, as such, constitute a trans-Canada highway.
This project has been envisaged for many years, and it is considered that the time is now appropriate to proceed with it. When first contemplated it was conceived as a highway from Halifax to Vancouver, but it is now proposed that it shall extend from Victoria, on Vancouver island, to St. John's, Newfoundland, and also embrace Prince Edward Island.
The highway, when completed, will remain the property of the respective provincial governments, who will assume their normal highway responsibilities with respect to it, such as maintenance and snow removal. In effect, therefore, this legislation will enable the federal government to assist provinces in highway construction.
I would like to point out to the minister that the increase in motor traffic and motive power in Canada has developed much faster than many of us thought would be the case, and perhaps even faster than the minister or the officials of his department considered likely. I believe that at this time a new deal should be made and the municipalities taken into consideration, as well as the provinces, in regard to the proper maintenance of these highways. The minister did point out at one time that federal contribution to the completion of the trans-Canada highway would amount to as much as 70 per cent of the total, but I will deal with that later.
Some of that expenditure covered the cost of the old road as well as the new and probably his department has now a better understanding that further help and assistance towards the completion of this road is now required. His department should offer some encouragement to the provinces to enable them to complete this highway and they should also offer something in the way of maintenance. This highway will stretch all across Canada and will pose a major problem to each of the provinces which it crosses. We must have more push and more encouragement from the Department of Public Works.
The minister mentioned during the speech from which I have already quoted that the project had been envisaged for many years. In fact, I remember one speech he made in the house in which he stated that the government had a large package of public works

on the shelf waiting for the time when it would be required to create work and wages for the masses. I believe that time has arrived now and if there is any doubt in the minister's mind I would ask him to look at the unemployment relief lists of the different towns and cities all across Canada. If he still does not think the time is ripe to take some of these packages off the shelf, then surely he will agree that the time has arrived when we must have a trans-Canada highway. That project would help provide employment all across Canada. We must have it speeded up more in the future than it has been in the past, and we require that speed-up now.
We accelerated the program last year but even acceleration is not sufficient to complete this program within the seven-year period mentioned in 1949. When this program was started, after many years of consultation, it was considered that it would extend over a seven-year period. Four years of that time has now elapsed and less than 800 miles of this 5,000-mile highway has been completed. That leaves 4,200 miles yet to be constructed. At the rate of the last four years it will take 21 more years to complete this program, despite the fact that this highway is badly needed now.
I would urge the minister to make a special effort to get Quebec to sign on the dotted line, because it will not look very good in three or four years' time if we have the highway all across Canada with the exception of a large chunk of Quebec.
I would like to refer again to the minister's speech on November 28, 1949, as reported at page 2329 of Hansard. At that time he said that something in the neighbourhood of $300 million would be required for the 5,000 miles of the highway, and the federal government's share would be $150 million. The minister also pointed out that there was an average cost of $60,000 per mile for new construction as well as for the highway already built. Of the amount of money voted, 30 per cent has already been spent and only 17 per cent of the road completed. I would now like to quote from his remarks at the bottom of page 2329. The minister said:
Let us take, for example, a province where $20 million would be needed to complete the highway, and where that province has already spent $8 million on portions of highway which will be part of the trans-Canada highway route. The federal government contribution for the new construction would be $10 million plus 50 per cent of costs previously incurred, or $4 million, for a total contribution of $14 million. If the province applies this contribution of $4 million against the cost of completing the highway, federal money in the $20 million expenditure would amount to $14 million, or 70 per cent. On the other hand, the payment for
Supply-Public Works roads already constructed may be applied elsewhere, as determined by the province, but it is my hope that the provincial governments will use it in such a way that the maximum amount of development and the maximum amount of employment will result.
A return I received a few days ago showed! that the cost per mile has not been $60,000, as the minister estimated in 1949, but $107,344 per mile. That figure is on the basis of the amount of money spent and the miles of road completed.
We all know, of course, that the cost of any project of such magnitude as the trans-Canada highway must cost much more per mile for the first year's operation than it would cost on the average a year or so after a start has been made, but I believe this expenditure to date is out of all proportion to what the road should cost. Officials of the Department of Public Works have already provided a great deal of assistance. Last year they provided 38 engineers, 5 technical officers, 4 draftsmen, and 5 survey assistants, and the travelling expenses for these men amounted to $61,000. According to the estimates, they have indulged in photography, for I see an item here for "films, broadcasting and advertising" and opposite that there is an amount of $23,000. It seems to me it would be time enough to take pictures, and broadcast and advertise, when the road is much nearer completion. As things stand at present it will be 21 years before it is completed.
According to an announcement by the department, the work was speeded up last year and contracts were let for $46,343,500. This was $12 million above the 1952 figure. Would this speed-up put on last year have anything to do with the 1953 election? Although it looks very much like it, I trust this was not the case, and that that speed-up will extend well into 1956 and this road will then be completed. If the government is going to dilly-dally along with this project and just put on a speed-up each election year, there can be no doubt that it will take 21 years to complete.
However, I am glad to know that all the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, have signed the agreement and I trust Quebec will sign sometime next year at the latest so that the minister will not have the excuse three years from now that the highway was not completed because one province did not sign the agreement. I am sure that every member of this house and the country is anxious to have this work done at the earliest possible moment as the need is great and the progress of the country requires much more road to be built in the future than has been built in the past. We hope that the speed of last year

Supply-Public Works will be accelerated and that this highway building program will not be accelerated for election years only. I trust that the cost per mile will get down to where it belongs, to the estimate that the minister made in the first place. It should not exceed $60,000 per mile.
I know the minister will say that the provinces have everything to do with the construction. I should like him to tell the house what the fifty-two officials of his department are doing in spending $61,000 in travelling expenses and also $23,000 for films, broadcasting and advertising. They have also spent $1 million in the national parks and have not built any road there at all in spite of the fact that roads through national parks are to be constructed and paid for 100 per cent by the federal government. One province has already spent $8 million for a road which will be part of the trans-Canada highway and is spending $10 million for new construction this year.
That is not our statement. That is your own.

There is no doubt about it- and I think the minister will agree with me -that construction of the trans-Canada highway has not been accelerated. It has not gone along as fast as it should have if it is going to be a seven-year program. In four years there has only been 800 miles of road built. At the rate of construction last year it will take fourteen years to finish it. As I said before, I think it is up to the department to give the provinces some encouragement, and I think there should be a new conference with all the provinces, all those that are interested in a road-building program, and the municipalities in each province which the road will go through should be brought into the conference. You should see if you cannot work out some new and better agreement to speed up construction of the trans-Canada highway.

I wonder whether I might say at this moment that there is a later item, 397, under which I think the trans-Canada highway might be more appropriately discussed and under which I would be very glad indeed to discuss it. I think I should say in reply to this speech that I find it a very strange one indeed and one that might more appropriately have been made in the legislature of Ontario or some other provincial government. My hon. friend well knows, because he indicated that he has read the legislation which he himself helped to pass, that the Trans-Canada Highway Act is enabling, that the responsibility for the construction of the highway rests with the provincial governments, and

that to the extent that they build the highway we are obligated by the act of parliament to contribute half the cost of construction.
We have been doing everything we can to urge on the provincial governments the desirability of making haste within the terms of the agreement. It is a seven-year period, and as recently as last December I wrote every provincial minister concerned under the terms of the agreements we have with nine of the ten provinces reminding them that the legislation would lapse on December 9, 1956, and that beyond that date parliament had given the government no authority to participate in sharing the cost of the trans-Canada highway. I reminded them that four years of the construction period have already elapsed, that only three remain, and that unless they accelerate their programs of construction they will not complete the highway in the time available to them. As I said, I also reminded them that we have no authority whatever beyond that date.
What more we can do to urge the provincial governments to meet the obligations which they themselves assumed under the terms of this agreement, I do not know. But those are the terms given to us by parliament, and I can assure all hon. members that there is no lack of desire on our part to get on with this construction program. I well recognize that in a province such as Ontario, for example, the trans-Canada highway is a very small percentage of their total highway construction program. But it is their responsibility to decide how much attention and how much effort they wish to focus on the trans-Canada highway and to what extent they wish to emphasize other phases of their highway construction program.
I have referred to Ontario on several occasions because that is perhaps the key link in any trans-Canada highway chain. There are sections in Ontario that have not been graded, and if we are going to enable automobile traffic to pass in relative comfort from one coast of Canada to the other it is absolutely essential that the link in the chain through the province of Ontario be completed. There are other provinces that have parts of the trans-Canada highway route still to be graded, but all hon. members know that Ontario is the key province in the chain of the trans-Canada highway agreement.

I should like to ask the
minister whether he does not think that the federal government should contribute something to the provinces toward maintaining this highway on account of the increase in

motor traffic that has taken place since 1949 when the agreement was first made? Give them some encouragement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would this particular question not come more properly when we reach the item concerning the trans-Canada highway? I am by no means saying that the question is out of order, but it does appear to me that particular questions would come more properly when the item is called.
I have got a lot more questions for that time, but I should like to have this one answered now. When does the minister think the highway will be finished?

I can only say to the hon.
nember what I have said to the provincial governments on many occasions, that this parliament has passed legislation which enables the federal government to participate with provincial governments under the trans-Canada highway agreements until December 9, 1956. Beyond that we have no authority. The terms of the legislation are specific. They enable the federal government to pay 50 per cent of the cost of construction, and it is clearly set forth that the maintenance of the road once it is constructed is the responsibility of the provinces in the same way as ownership of the highway. There was a matter of provincial jurisdiction and autonomy involved and we made it clear, and it was the wish of all provincial governments, that ownership and maintenance of the highway should be provincial matters.
The minister has not answered my question. He has officials who must have some idea. They must have given some thought to the matter. When do they think the highway will be completed?
It depends on the provinces.

I guess it depends on the
moon.

All I can say is there has been agreement. If one can say that the provinces entered into the agreement in good faith and propose to live up to its terms, then the trans-Canada highway will be completed by December 9, 1956.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the extemporaneous speech of the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, but I want to discuss a matter of policy which is not covered under any other item of the estimates of the Department of Public Works except this one. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would explain to the house what policy is followed by the federal government in determining when they will
Supply-Public Works make a contribution toward the cost of building bridges. I was very interested in a question asked only yesterday by a member from Ontario as to the contribution by the federal government towards the cost of a bridge in Ontario. As I understood the minister's answer, it was that because the government owned or controlled a canal the government were prepared to pay one-third of the cost of the bridge.
That brings me to an important question. What is the policy of the government and what determines the government's action with respect to whether or not they will contribute towards the cost of construction of bridges? I believe the minister knows right now what I have in mind. I am discussing the Marpole bridge in the city of Vancouver. This bridge crosses a navigable river which comes under the control and jurisdiction of the federal government because it is a navigable river.
There is only one airport for the city of Vancouver, which has a twofold value. First, it has a commercial value. I believe that it is one of the most used airports in the Dominion of Canada. In view of the fact that Vancouver is on the Pacific coast, the airport has an interest in the realm of defence. This bridge is obsolete. It has been knocked out time after time by tugs and log booms. There is no question about the need for a new bridge. From my studies and my knowledge of the situation, Mr. Chairman, I am going to say that basically the bridge is a municipal and provincial responsibility. I admit that.
There is the issue, however, that the bridge crosses a navigable river and provides the only access to the airport for commercial or defence purposes, or offence, if you want to put it that way, on the west coast. I believe these considerations can reasonably bring the bridge within the realm of federal government interests. I understand the federal government is now in the process of negotiating, or has completed negotiations, to take over the Vancouver airport. I do not know whether or not it has been taken over as yet, but I understand there are negotiations to that end and the federal government has made an offer to the city of Vancouver.
I am certain I could talk for about an hour on this subject. I do not believe I have to do that because I am sure the Minister of Public Works knows the importance of that bridge. I am convinced that if there were an offer of assistance from the federal government it would accelerate the building of what I believe is one of the most necessary bridges in the entire Dominion of Canada. Although

Supply-Public Works I may have to say more about it later, and that depends upon the minister's answer, I am going to go back to what I started to say. What is the policy, and how is it determined, in regard to grants for the construction of bridges?
I shall put the question directly through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of Public Works. What negotiations have there been in the past or are there now, and can the federal government assist British Columbia in the construction of a vital bridge over the Fraser river at Marpole?

Mr. Chairman, I would
imagine that there are as many circumstances that have a bearing on policy as there are potential bridges or existing bridges. Generally, though, there are some cornerstones of policy. If a bridge is entirely within the area of a province, then it is normally regarded as a provincial responsibility. If the bridge is over interprovincial or international waters, then there is some reason for the federal government's participation and the federal government normally does participate. One example of that is the proposed Pembroke bridge, which is under discussion now, and with respect to which the federal government has told the governments of Ontario and Quebec that we are prepared to participate and co-ordinate the work if they wish to go forward with the structure.
There is another bridge across an international water at St. Stephen, New Brunswick, which I have in mind, and for which the federal government is also ready to pay a part of the cost. The fact that the water is navigable does not necessarily mean the federal government is responsible for sharing the cost of a bridge over it. Normally the federal government has a decision to make as to whether the navigable water should or not be bridged; that is a matter for decision under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
In the case of the bridge over the Burlington canal, there were many circumstances. This canal was built by the old commission of works, I think it was called, before confederation, and has always been regarded as a federal structure. It has been maintained by the federal government since confederation. There is a railway bridge over the canal now as well as a highway bridge. It was a double bascule bridge, but one side of it was knocked out by a ship. There is a temporary fixed bridge there now. One side is still bascule, which can be raised to enable navigation to pass through. This bridge was built by the federal government. It is maintained by the federal government, so


the federal government already has an interest and responsibility there because of that involvement in the bridge.
The government of Ontario has asked permission to build a high level bridge over the canal to facilitate the flow of the very large and developing volume of traffic that must move over the canal to complete the circuit of travel. We have told the Ontario government that we are prepared to participate with them in that expenditure up to a maximum of one-third. We were prompted in that by two basic considerations, and we made one of them a condition of our participation. The first was that we be permitted to abandon our present bridge over the canal for which we are responsible and which we maintain. The other consideration was the requirement of navigation through the canal which was built by the federal government or the forerunner of the federal government.
The requirements of navigation make it necessary to build a much more expensive bridge than would be required were there no need to consider navigation. The reason is that a high level bridge will be required rather than the low level bridge which otherwise could have been built. For these reasons we felt there was a federal government responsibility. In British Columbia, at Marpole, the river is navigable and we are quite willing to give permission to British Columbia to build a suitable bridge over the river, having regard to the requirements of navigation. The water is purely within provincial boundaries. There seems to be no federal government involvement other than the potential one of the airport my hon. friend mentioned.
We have, to date, told the government of British Columbia that there is no federal government responsibility with respect to the bridge, and that we cannot participate in the cost.
Have you told the province of British Columbia that you will not make any grant? Do I understand that?
That is what we have told the British Columbia government.

Is that not a change of policy? I understand that in the past discussions, extending over two years, there was an offer by the federal government to participate in the expenditure. Has that been withdrawn?

Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of any offer. I know the history of this bridge since I have been Minister of Public Works. Since that time, in correspondence with the minister of highways of the government of British Columbia, I told him that in

my opinion there was no federal government responsibility, and that I could see no grounds for federal government participation.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid there is some misunderstanding on the part of members of the cabinet. This subject has been discussed for quite a few years. I have here a press clipping of September 18, 1946, bearing the heading "Ottawa to aid City on Bridge to Airport", and stating as follows:
The federal government will share in the cost of a new high level bridge at Marpole-to serve the municipal airport

with the city and Richmond, Reconstruction Minister C. D. Howe told city council at a private meeting this morning.
A report covering the proposed location, type and clearance of the span is to be prepared by civic, provincial and dominion engineers.
This was the highlight of three announcements made by Mr. Howe.
That was nearly eight years ago.
Then, I have here another clipping from the News-Herald, of June 11, 1949, under the heading "Federal Aid Promised For New Bridge", and stating:
The federal government is willing to put up one-third the cost of a high level bridge across the Fraser river, says Arthur Laing, Liberal candidate in Vancouver South.
And this basis of a third by the dominion, a third by the province and a third by the city has been the basis all the way through- at least it was in the beginning. The article continues:
He said Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, had told1 him the money is available and the government is only waiting for city and provincial authorities to decide on a site.
Then, in 1950 I find an article indicating the holding of a conference on this subject in Ottawa. This article is dated at Ottawa, March 31, 1950, under the heading "Bridge Talks Open", and states:
Vancouver and B.C. government representatives met a federal cabinet member today in the first round of the city's fight for a new $10,000,000 high-level bridge to span the Fraser river at the foot of Oak.
B.C. Works Minister Carson, accompanied by Aid. J. D. Cornett and city engineer John Oliver, met federal works minister Fournier.
"We're just getting into the problem," said Mr. Carson, adding the delegation would meet other ministers within the next few days. Negotiations might easily continue after the delegation returned to B.C., he added.
"A very fair reception," said Aid. Cornett.
Remember, this was four years ago. The article continues:
The delegation had received strong support from B.C.'s federal members, Mr. Carson said.
Works minister Fournier, trade minister Howe and transport minister Chevrier are representing the federal government.
Supply-Public Works
Then, I find a dispatch dated November 28, 1951, under the heading "Ottawa's Offer dims Marpole Span Hopes", and stating:
Ottawa will pay only $400,000 if and when a new bridge is built over the Fraser at Marpole, B.C.'s cabinet minister in the federal government, Hon. Robert Mayhew, said today.
Mr. Mayhew said this assistance was offered by trade minister Howe and "still stands."
That was the statement in 1951 by the then representative of British Columbia in the dominion cabinet. Yet we have the present Minister of Public Works saying that the dominion will not pay one cent.
Mr. Chairman, that simply is not good enough. This bridge is used primarily for traffic to the airport-an airport which, I believe, does more business than any other in Canada. Certainly if there is any other doing more business, it would only be the airport at Dorval. Time and again people are held up by reason of the fact that this old Marpole bridge is open, perhaps to let a scow or a tug through, and it opens hundreds of times each year. I think it was only last year that the Prime Minister was delayed for half an hour or so because this span had to be opened.
As the minister knows, navigation has the right of way. When a tug comes along towing a scow loaded with sawdust, or anything of that nature, all traffic to the airport has to stop while the bridge is opened. Traffic cannot continue until the tug and scow have passed through.
If that situation existed in Montreal, Toronto or Ottawa the people in those districts would be frantic; it simply could not happen. These cities are so near the centre of government that things of that kind would not be tolerated. I suggest to the minister there is no reason why nearly a million people in greater Vancouver should be subjected to a situation of this kind. The federal government cannot get away from some responsibility. Perhaps the provincial government should take the lead-and the provincial government has announced its willingness to do that. The city of Vancouver has been willing to help all the way through.
To hear the Minister of Public Works for Canada say that he and his department are not interested, and that the federal government will not do anything about the bridge, is simply going back on a promise made years ago, and repeated year after year by responsible ministers in this same government.
I do suggest that the minister should take another look at this situation. The only possible excuse for his attitude today is that he does not know the facts, and that he does

Supply-Public Works not know what has been going on right here in Ottawa in connection with this bridge. I hope we will have assurance from him today that he will take the matter up with his colleagues and that, as a result, Ottawa will agree to do its fair share toward building a proper and modern bridge over the north arm of the Fraser river.

May I add a further word. I am grateful to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra for having placed on record the newspaper comment.
When I spoke earlier I did not say some of the things that perhaps I should have said.
1 think it is known to the minister that for twenty years I was in the British Columbia legislature, and that during twelve of those years I had the honour of leading His Majesty's loyal opposition as a member from the city of Vancouver. As a member from Vancouver and also as leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition in that legislature I was, ex officio, a member of the cabinet-"ex officio";
I stress that.
However, as a result of holding that honour I did know something about the negotiations conducted in matters of this kind. I want to say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister, that in the past few years this matter has been of great importance to Vancouver and the province of British Columbia. It was always our understanding that the federal government was prepared to make a financial contribution toward the construction of a bridge at Marpole. The only problem ever presented to us in our meetings with the city council of Vancouver, or from a legislative standpoint, was as to where the bridge should be

whether at Marpole, Oak street or Fraser. The remarks of the minister this afternoon are the first indication I have had that they were not prepared to make any contribution financially.
I can only repeat my own words and emphasize this. Without any question of doubt there is a responsibility on the federal government. Without any question of doubt there is a commitment of more than one cabinet minister of the Liberal government that they would contribute toward the cost of a new bridge. I just want to add my word once again. We have got to have it. There is no question about it. In peace and in war we have got to have that new bridge.
I ask the minister to go over the history, study the situation and come forward with no less than one-third of the cost of a new bridge at Marpole.

In connection with this item,
I was pleased when the hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra and Vancouver East


raised the bridge question. In so far as the bridge is concerned, there is no doubt in the minds of British Columbians, particularly those on the lower mainland, that the federal authorities do have a responsibility, but I shall bring that problem to light later on. The hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, mentioned highways. We have a highway problem in the Yellowhead pass that will probably be dealt with by one of my associates. However, my problem in this instance happens to be something having to do with remarks that were made on March 12 by certain hon. members who intimated that this government was using electioneering as a political football: that is, that you had to vote Liberal in order to get what you wanted. I know a lot of people say, "Oh, well, that is all foolish", and so on; but in view of the fact that all those past governments or cabinet ministers have indicated that they were desirous of helping the provincial government and the city of Vancouver to build the Marpole bridge, one just begins to wonder whether there is not some element of truth in the suggestion, in so far as the province of British Columbia is concerned, on account of its having changed its particular provincial politics. I hear an hon. gentleman say, "Nonsense". It probably is. I would not place any credence in it, sir, if it were not for the fact that in the Surrey Leader of March 25, on page 7, I read this:
Liberal comeback soon, Mott tells Surrey club.
I for one know Mr. Mott very well. I have every reason to respect his thoughts and his ideas. He was a valuable servant of this government and he was a valuable servant of the people of New Westminster. My quarrel has never been with William Mott or with anyone else concerned with that same gentleman who served his province and his city so well. But I should like to read this:
William Mott spoke on the future of the Liberal party in British Columbia at the annual meeting of the Liberal Association for Ocean Park, Crescent Beach and Elgin. Meeting was held in the Legion hall at Crescent on March 12, and there was an excellent attendance.
Mr. Mott feels that there is every hope of the party making a comeback in the near future. He also stated that last year a large amount of money had been expended by the federal government in Surrey, but that this year, since George Hahn has been in office, there has been none allocated with the exception of the Annacis Island development.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if that is not a suggested reason why I should not have been elected I would like to know what it is, and I should like to have an answer to it. Certainly, it does not come out and say that you must vote Liberal or you will get no public works, but the intimation is definitely

there. I do know the Minister of Public Works well enough to realize that those are not his sentiments. At least, I have reason to believe that those are not his sentiments.
I believe such a charge should be refuted, and in no uncertain terms. That is the only reason for my rising at this time. He has treated me quite well so far as I am concerned as an individual, but it is up to him to let those who were defeated know that that is not his policy or the policy of his government, if it is not so; otherwise, we must accept the suggestion that because the province of British Columbia turned out the Liberal government and elected a Social [DOT]Credit government, no further help is coming from this government.
Mr. Chairman, may I just say one further word on the Marpole bridge before we leave it and get into maritime matters?
Do not leave it; give us something.

What I said about my conversations and correspondence with the government of British Columbia represents my thinking on the problem. It was arrived at after a careful search of the files, during which I found no binding commitment, nor indeed any commitment of any kind, requiring the federal government to participate in the cost of the Marpole bridge. I have been hearing about these reported commitments through the press, such as that quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I simply wish to assure the committee that if my predecessor here or any of my other colleagues in good faith have committed the federal government to participation in that bridge, they may be assured that that commitment will be honoured.
I did not get an answer to my question regarding the inference.
I did not-
Do I understand that if there was any statement or impression left by any of the predecessors of my hon. friend of financial assistance to the building of the Marpole bridge he would honour it?
I said that if there is any valid commitment on the part of my-
