speechtext: That is well protected.

I do not want to hedge on these words. If my predecessor, or any of my colleagues, speaking on their responsibilities as members of the cabinet, have said that we will participate in the cost of building the Marpole bridge, then we will honour the
Supply-Public Works commitment; but I have been able to find on the files no record of any such commitment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Royal.

I know the hon. members who have been trying to rise have a much greater contribution to make to this subject than I have. However, I feel I have my rights. I have been up two or three times. I want to discuss the general problem. I think there is a great misunderstanding as to just what the federal responsibility is in the matter of bridges. This Marpole bridge is an excellent example, I should think, of cases where the federal government should give assistance.
I was in Halifax a few days ago and I noted that the bridge across Halifax harbour is pretty well near completion. They expect to have it finished this year. I understand that the bridge across Halifax harbour has been the responsibility of the federal government, the local government and the city of Halifax.
Just the latter two, Mr. Chairman, the provincial government and the municipalities.
The federal government has made no contribution at all?
No contribution, no.
It is understood at Halifax that the federal government was making a contribution.
A great many people think that, but it is not correct.

The federal government is getting a lot of credit for something that it is not doing, which has been true in the past. An hon. member mentioned bridges connecting different provinces. In the past I have brought to the attention of this department a bridge which the people of Campbell-ton, N.B., and Cross Point in Quebec feel should be constructed. Has the minister anything to say in connection with this bridge? Is there any possibility of a bridge being constructed in that vicinity in the near future?

Mr. Chairman, I may say what the situation is there. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska has been very much interested in this matter, and not long ago he led a delegation to see me. We have written to the government of Quebec and to the government of New Brunswick telling them that if they are anxious to have a bridge built across-

Across the bay of Chaleur, at Campbellton.

Supply-Public Works

Yes, at Campbellton. We told them that if they are anxious to have a bridge built across the bay at Campbellton, we are prepared to co-ordinate the work there, and are certainly prepared to give favourable consideration to financial participation.
It would be a three-party arrangement?

Yes; it would be a three-party arrangement. The government of New Brunswick seemed to be quite interested. The government of Quebec at that time was involved in its legislative program and the reply we received was that they had too much work on hand at that particular moment to devote their attention to this bridge but that they hoped to be in a position to consider it at a later date, at which time they would communicate with us.

I have just a brief word to say. I know this bridge in Vancouver. I think I have a right to know the airfield. The worst bottleneck I have seen in Canada was leading up to that Marpole bridge. When I was out there the information I obtained was that the city of Vancouver expected to sell the airfield to the dominion government and that the money received would be used in building the bridge. I do not know how far that matter goes, but that is the information I had. As to the need for that bridge, I say it is one of Canada's outstanding needs, but I trust the minister to be fair.

I must thank the minister for providing for a public building in my constituency. When the minister was before the committee on March 12 trying to get this item through, I mentioned the fact that a year ago provision had been made for a public building at Carrot River. The Minister of Agriculture is in the chamber and I am sure he will agree with me that Carrot River is a very important centre. Can the minister indicate whether it was an oversight that this item is not in the estimates this year whereas a year ago apparently provision was made for the building of a public building there? In a letter written to me on February 5 the Postmaster General mentioned that a public building was needed very badly. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are also servicing quite a large area. Can the minister say whether it was an oversight that Carrot River was overlooked in the supplementary estimates which were brought down at the end of the month or whether plans can be proceeded with for the construction of a public building at this important centre?

No, Mr. Chairman; it certainly was not an oversight. On a previous occasion I outlined to my hon. friend the policy of the department in not providing funds in the estimates for work we are not prepared to undertake during the year under consideration. That is the position we are in at Carrot River. It is a matter for future planning before we shall be able to undertake the work there.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I think we would have a little bit more orderly discussion here if we discussed these various provincial projects under the particular vote for the province concerned.

What I have to say is not a provincial matter. It has to do with the charge that was made in connection with a particular item respecting a Liberal policy. I want to know whether or not the minister wants to let the inference stand wherein Mr. Mott suggests that the reason I have not had any public works in my district is that the area did not vote Liberal. Is that the policy or is it not?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether Mr. Mott or anybody else made such a statement. These are just reports which I know the hon. member is relaying here to me in good faith; but until I know the context and the spirit in which the remarks were made, I could not pass judgment on them. I may say that all these projects are treated on their merits.
It is a press report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the general administration of public works.

That is the situation. I should like to be within my rights here. I think it is a matter of administration as to the policy of the government, as set down, whereby they are going to allocate public works at certain places.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

In this report was it stated specifically that the reason there had not been this allocation was that the voters had elected Mr. Hahn, or was it that they had elected a Social Credit supporter? Was it a distinction as between two members or was it a distinction as to party?
I am sorry, but I passed the report over to the reporter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind the hon. member that we are discussing the first item, item No. 360, of the Department of Public Works. I have allowed a fairly generous discussion, as I think hon. members will agree, but I cannot allow this discussion to go any further. I would ask the hon. members to confine themselves to a discussion of this department and not to indulge in a discussion of political matters.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. If you cannot discuss a department's policy on the first item, which is administration, just where are you going to discuss it? That is not a difficult question for the minister to answer. I have known the minister for a good long time and, as far as I am concerned, I do not think he takes politics into consideration when allotting these different projects. But let him say so now. Now is the time to make this point clear, particularly in the instance referred to by the hon. member who was speaking just a moment ago. There is no difficulty in the matter for the minister. Let him say that Mott was telling something that is not true or that he was telling the truth, one or the other.

If the hon. member wishes to take responsibility for statements he has seen in the press, he is acting on his own. I have already said-and I think my hon. friend heard me-that these projects are considered on their merits.
No politics in it.

When I raised the matter of the Marpole bridge I was discussing it under item 360 because there is no specific item which covers it. I want to raise one other matter of policy and ask the Minister of Public Works a question, in view of the situation in Canada, where even according to the Minister of Finance our first six months may be on a downgrade, but he hopes that the next six months will be on the upgrade, where we have at the present moment in the neighbourhood of 500,000 unemployed. That being the situation, whether it is in a recession or in prosperity-
Does my hon. friend not mean 500,000 applications for jobs? I think there is quite a distinction there.

That is right; 592,000 applications for jobs. If the minister wants me to put it that way, I will do so. What I am coming to is this. I cannot understand why, in the architects' drawings and specifications for public buildings being constructed by the
Supply-Public Works Dominion of Canada, we specify materials coming from outside of Canada. I refer in particular, of course, to the post office in Vancouver. With all the beautiful granite and marble of varying types in Canada, why should it be necessary to specify-or why should it be done-in any government specifications that any material coming from outside of Canada should be used in the construction of public buildings? I think that is an important matter at any time, but it is a particularly important matter at a time when we have 592,000 applications for employment in the Dominion of Canada. I believe I know Canada fairly well. I know its products and resources fairly well, and for the life of me, Mr. Chairman, I cannot understand why the dominion government, through the Department of Public Works and their architectural branch, plan a building and specify marble which has to come from Italy, or some other country. As far as I am concerned it simply does not make sense. I admit it may be beautiful. You have only to inspect this House of Commons and you will find marble from many countries, but you will also find throughout this entire building granite and marble which is a product of this dominion. I cannot see why that marble and that granite produced in Canada are not good enough for the government in its specifications. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister whether this is strictly a matter of policy, and why, in the specifications of a multimillion dollar construction such as the Vancouver post office, they specified imported Italian marble. We have marble finishers in Canada who could be employed if we used our own marble and granite. Why cannot we have a policy of using the produce of Canada in public works constructions?

Mr. Chairman, as a matter of policy the specifications of the Department of Public Works require Canadian materials consistent with economy. The particular building to which my hon. friend referred was designed for the Department of Public Works by very competent architects from Vancouver. In order to get the quality and the colour of the marble in certain public areas they specified requirements that could be met only by importing Italian marble.
Why?

Because of the type of granular structure and the appearance of the marble. It is a very small part of the total cost of the building. The total value of the marble purchased and worked in Italy will be of the order of about $60,000 which is a very small percentage of a building cost of
3946	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works some $9 million. We have endeavoured-and, I believe, succeeded to a very large extent- to use domestic materials in public works structures. There are instances from time to time where, on grounds of economy or for some technical reason, foreign materials are included; but by and large I think hon. members would agree, if they had the opportunity of examining the specifications and the tenders submitted, that we have achieved a pretty good measure of success in having local materials used in these projects.

Surely it is like buying an oil painting such as a Rembrandt in order to show our people in Canada some of the beauties from other lands. The texture of the marble must be worth observing and it seems to me this is no doubt part of an educational campaign to show our people in the form of these public buildings the things which come from other parts of the world. That policy has been carried on for years and possibly the sort of material required cannot be obtained in Canada.
But that is not the point. Did the minister say that this building will cost $9 million?

Yes, of the order of $9
million.

And the minister informs us
that out of the $9 million structure it is required to have a $60,000 importation of Italian marble. But that does not make sense to me, Mr. Chairman. The importation of $60,000 worth of Italian marble may not be a considerable item, but I would point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the marble polishers and granite finishers in Canada could have nine months' work on that amount.
No.
Yes, I believe they would.

I understand the polishing
in Canada would represent about $37,000 and perhaps give work to some 45 men for about three months.

The minister has not contradicted me one bit. As a matter of fact, he has helped me considerably and I appreciate that. That work could go to the people of Canada and they would reap the benefit from the expenditure of this $60,000 item out of a total expenditure of $9 million. But I still cannot understand why we should import Italian marble.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. When
this item was last being considered by the
IMr. Winters.]

committee on March 12 I was about to make some comments when the committee rose. I propose to make these comments now. First of all, I would like to congratulate the minister on his appointment to the very important portfolio of Minister of Public Works. I believe the choice is a very happy one and for a variety of reasons I am pleased that he holds that portfolio. To begin with, he is an engineer and I think the ministry of public works is a job which should be held by an engineer. I am also glad to see this portfolio come to the maritime provinces, and, without being facetious, I believe another reason why the present minister is highly qualified to hold the post is that he received at least part of his education at the university from which I myself graduated.
A great man.

We are both great men. I
think perhaps the Prime Minister made the best possible selection when casting about for an appointee to fill this position, particularly when one considers the limitations placed upon his freedom of choice.
The minister has a very important task before him, because I believe the Department of Public Works is one of the most important portfolios in this government. It is one with which every part of the country is intimately concerned. I was pleased to hear the minister say that it is hoped that in future more of the construction work being carried out on behalf of the government will be undertaken by his department. I think that is as it should be, and I will be looking forward to the day when all public building construction, or as much as possible, will be done by the Department of Public Works. The minister's job is an important and difficult one for another reason. It is especially difficult because I think his department perhaps ranks lowest of all government departments in public esteem. As a result of its past history people have not had too much confidence in it. I think the general feeling of the Canadian people with respect to this department in past years is aptly expressed in an article found on page 6 of Maclean's magazine of November 1. The article is written by Blair Fraser and reads in part as follows:
Normally the Minister of Public Works knows a great deal about politics. Now, for the first time in human memory, he knows something about public works. Public works has been, in fact, the last surviving puddle-
He does not say how big the puddle is.
-of the great dismal swamp of politics and patronage which once engulfed the whole government service. There hasn't been an actual scandal

in the department since the 1890's, when the notorious McGreevy affair exposed a nasty situation, but though old-fashioned graft was cleaned up, old-fashioned patronage was not. Public works remained proverbial, in and out of the government service, for inefficiency and general ineptitude. This was not the fault of the harried handful of competent civil servants trying to run the department. They had to work with the blunt instruments the politicians gave them, and as the years went by they got more and more discouraged and resigned to defeat.
I am delighted to be able to hope that the department is now starting with a clean sheet and that things will be different in the future. Before I go further, may I say that I sincerely wish the minister and his deputy minister success in their attempts to bring about this very necessary improvement. Both today and on Maroh 12 a great deal of concern has been expressed about the possibility that certain parts of the country are discriminated against simply because they see fit to elect to parliament members who are not supporters of the government. I trust that is not so and that it never was so, but I know for a fact that a very large percentage of the Canadian people believe that it is so. There is no denying that they have been encouraged in that belief from time to time by certain people in this country merely for their own personal benefit.
I was delighted to hear the minister say that when consideration is given to new public works decisions will be reached on the merits of the work in question and the merits alone. I was delighted to hear the minister say that because if he makes that understood at every turn he will have gone a long way toward improving the esteem in which his department is held by the general public.
There is another matter that I wish to refer to briefly, and I was pleased to hear the minister say that there will be a change in this connection. I refer to the custom in the past of putting items in the estimates that apparently have had no meaning. It has been customary year after year for items to appear in the estimates and for the money not to be spent. The explanation that has been given is that some time before the estimates come before parliament again someone might be moved by some whim to start on some public work, and that therefore it was nice and convenient to have an item in the estimates so that they would have authority for doing so if the occasion should arise. If estimates are meaningless it makes a mockery out of considering them, and I am pleased to hear the minister say that in the future items will appear in his estimates only when it is contemplated that the work will be proceeded with in the year
Supply-Public Works ahead and before there is another opportunity to present a similar item to parliament. But that has been far from the case in the past.
As an example, I should like to cite the case of the public building in Charlottetown. To satisfy my own curiosity I examined the estimates of the last several years and I found that an item has appeared for this building in every year since 1947 to date, with a cumulative total of $1,500,000. As yet there is no visible sign of any building being constructed. I am delighted to know that the project will go forward in the year ahead. But the unfortunate thing about the recurrence of such items in the estimates is the fact that our budget is based on the estimates, and taking only the case to which I have referred the Canadian people have already been taxed to the extent of $1,500,000 for a building the construction of which has not even commenced. To me that is not good business.
I think the estimates should be real and meaningful estimates of the money actually to be spent in the year ahead. Then funds can be raised to meet the proposed expenditures from year to year. I think that is only common sense and good business. I believe the Canadian people are sick and tired of paying real taxes for meaningless estimates to build phantom buildings. There is nothing else I want to say at the present time except that I note that under this item there is a considerable increase in the amount set aside for wages. That is caused in part, I understand, by the fact that the staff has been increased by twenty-five and partly by an increase in the rates of wages. I would be very pleased if the minister, when convenient, would explain a little more fully how much of the increase is for increases in rates of wages, how much is for additional members of the staff, why additional staff is necessary and whether the addition to the staff is an addition because the department is taking over work which was formerly done by other departments or whether it is really an increase in the total number of civil servants.

I am sorry to revert again to the Marpole bridge but I feel that as a former member of the British Columbia civil service I was in a position to know the feeling of the people in government circles and the people of Vancouver with respect to an understanding between the federal government, the government of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver. Certainly it was our understanding that if it had not been for the procrastination of the city of Vancouver the Marpole bridge would have been built long ago.

Supply-Public Works
I can clearly recall that the Hon. E. C. Carson, minister of public works at the time when I was deputy minister of education, told me there was a definite commitment on the part of this government and all that was standing in the way of proceeding with the building of the bridge was the question of a site. He told me also that three engineers had unanimously chosen the Fraser avenue site, but they could get no agreement from the officials of the city of Vancouver.
It is true that there is no legal obligation on the part of the federal to make a contribution towards this bridge. I feel that is something we must remember. It is a matter of expediency or if you like an implied obligation on the part of this government to service the airport that caused the ministers of that day to agree that federal assistance be given, and that they were quite prepared to proceed on a three-way basis with the province and the city. That was the definite understanding.
A one-third contribution?

I am just giving my impression, Mr. Chairman, and the impression certainly of the most of the people of Vancouver and British Columbia. Certainly that was the impression in the minds of the officials of the provincial government. I feel I should say that. I hope that the minister will, as he has been urged by several speakers, take a second look to see if we cannot come to a settlement of this vexed question.

Before the item passes there are one or two questions I wanted to ask the minister. As he has said earlier, I realize that the expenditures deal with the current year and not the distant future. But upon looking over the details of the estimates I was unable to find any great increase in the amount of money that will be spent for harbours and wharves on lake Erie or lake Huron. I was looking into the future hoping that possibly in view of the proposed new seaway more attention would be paid to the facilities at these various ports. With the increasing cost of highway and railway transportation, I am hoping that water transportation on the great lakes will offer a cheaper alternative method of transportation than we have enjoyed in the past. As a consequence, I asked that question.
Upon going through the estimates of the Department of Public Works I found no mention of any item dealing with the seaway. I see item No. 444 in the Department of Transport deals with that but I presume a portion of the work will eventually be done by the Department of Public Works. I hope it is not out of order to mention that, with
[Mr. Fairey.)
all the negotiations and talk going on about the seaway, I am hoping it is not the policy of this government to try to get the United States to join with us in the building of the seaway. I believe that the policy of the government should be to do everything in its power to make it an all-Canadian seaway so we can have control of it, and it will not be one of those international things about which there is bickering all the time. We know what has happened to our tariffs. I just mention that in passing.
I see there is an item of $100,000 for the dock at Kagawong on Manitoulin island. I believe I mentioned that a year or two ago. Then we come down the great lakes and I notice there is an item of nearly $100,000 for Colchester and another item of $100,000 for Kingsville. However, I notice that there is only about $19,000 for Pelee island. Kingsville and Leamington are two ports that serve the Pelee area, but there are two docks on Pelee island, the north dock and the west dock. I have been there a good many times and know something about the area. It is increasing in importance, and there is a vast amount of agricultural wealth produced on the island. I believe these people are hoping that more improvements in the dock facilities will be made.
I suppose I really should not mention this but I heard the hon. member for New Westminster referring to political bait held out to constituencies. I feel that the minister does not want any part of that. He gets dragged into these things against his will. I was glad to hear him say that his decision as to proceeding with public works would be based on the merits of each case. I commend him for that statement. In passing I want to mention to him that during the heat of the by-election in Elgin reference was made to the fact that more could be gained for the constituency if a member on the government side were elected. Figures were brought forward that such was not the case. The new member for Elgin will be here next week, so I am not going into that any farther. Apparently the results would indicate that people do not like to be dealt with in that manner.

I should like to bring a matter to the attention of the committee that is of concern to all members. I refer to the shelf of public projects we were supposed to have back in 1945. I noticed from a perusal of the estimates before us there is an increase in the amount allotted this department over last year by $10 million. It is quite natural that those of us who feel that something of a dynamic nature should

be undertaken by this government to overcome the unemployment situation in this country are quite concerned about the loss in potential prosperity, if I may put it that way, due to the loss of man-hours.
Back in 1945 when I came into this house, Mr. Chairman, at the end of the war, I recall that we were faced with the question of: where do we go from here? The war was at an end and we were wondering whether the Canadian economy would retrogress into the conditions we experienced in the thirties. At that time I recall, as many other hon. members will, the government gave confirmation of the fact that they had a shelf of public projects which could be undertaken if the Canadian economy showed signs of lapsing into a condition which would bring about unemployment. This scheme of public projects sponsored by the federal government was to overcome that difficulty.
Upon returning to the House of Commons this year I find that apparently this shelf of public projects has either gone into the wastepaper basket or has been forgotten. I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that in Canada today we have a very grave unemployment situation. In excess of 500,000, nearly 600,000, people have registered for employment. If we want to prevent the loss of wealth which these people could produce for the Canadian economy, then it is the responsibility of the federal government to undertake a dynamic policy of public works. To make a mental calculation of what we are losing today in manhours one could take the very conservative figure of 500,000 unemployed on a five-day 40-hour week, and arrive at the colossal sum of 80 million man-hours per month that we lose.
Those of us in this group say that after all real wealth can be created only by the application of our labour force to our natural resources. One can see readily that there is nothing very dynamic in the present economic system of Canada if that is all the government has to offer. Therefore I urge the Minister of Public Works who, I know, is an excellent minister trying to do his part, to develop a public works program. I do not know what influence he has with his colleagues in the cabinet. We do know however that tremendous expenditures are being made for defence, reaching about $2 billion and, in the circumstances, I think it is reasonable, wise and expedient to use some of our public money in a vigorous public works program.
I suggest that in this connection the minister would do well to confer with his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and
Supply-Public Works that they consider what is involved in the protection of our people in a time of war when hydrogen bombs might be used. Anyone who has made any study of the subject knows that under our civil defence program there are no facilities with which we could protect ourselves in such event.
I do not know what the plans of the government were when they told us between 1945 and 1949 that they had a shelf of public works projects, but I am saying to the minister now that right at this moment it would be expedient for the government to give serious consideration to considering a real and dynamic program through which we will develop our resources and make use of that shelf of public projects by proceeding with slum clearance, the elimination of level crossings, and thus stamping out accidents at those crossings, and entering into commitments or agreements with the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the development of a program all along the line in the matter of public works. I should think this would be preferable to reducing the expenditures of last year or to the $130,776,751 indicated as the expenditures for this year.
If there are any public works projects on the shelf that could be proceeded with, in my opinion it would be expedient to go forward at once with them and thus eliminate some of the unemployment.
It is all very well for members of the House of Commons who are receiving their indemnities and who have financial security. But when we leave the House of Commons for the Easter vacation and return to our homes we will meet people whose incomes have fallen because they have been unable to sell their grain. And when the farmers are not in a position to employ help, there are many who are unemployed. To put the matter succinctly, we will find many who are unemployed. It is a most serious thing when one's income is cut off completely. The government should have sufficient vision and vitality to go ahead. If we are going to tell the world that this is a free world, and that we live in a dynamic economic society, then let us get busy and do something about it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Public Works one question in connection with the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East when he discussed the use of Italian marble in the new post office building at Vancouver. The minister will recall that I asked him a question on March 17 about this marble and he answered on March 19 indicating that Italian marble was to be used. Before plans or specifications of this kind involving the

Supply-Public Works
use of such articles from abroad are passed by the minister's department is there any attempt made to find out whether there are men unemployed in the districts where similar work is being done in Canada? Here we find men unemployed in Vancouver, and yet the minister has admitted this afternoon that if Canadian rather than Italian marble were used it would give employment to 45 men for three months. That is not something to laugh at. It means that 45 families would have had the benefit of three months' work.
When it comes to a question of whether 45 men should be given work, or whether we should have marble of a little finer texture in a post office, I think the only reasonable decision would be to give the men work. I presume what happened was that the Vancouver architect wanted to have a fine monument to himself, and with this in mind he called for the fine Italian marble. Then when the specifications reached Ottawa the officials here did not bother to make any change or to find out whether or not there were men in Vancouver who were out of work.
Is it the policy of the department to make inquiries about those who are out of work before it approves specifications which will mean giving work to people living in other countries?

Is any study made by the minister's experts as to the availability of products of a type similar to those to be imported? I ask that question because I believe there is in the constituency of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary quantities of marble and granite of similar texture and hardness to that imported from Italy. Was any investigation made on that point, or was there any study given to it?

Replying to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the answer is yes. All public projects are undertaken having due regard to the labour situation in the area. I think perhaps the hon. member may be placing the emphasis in the wrong place. On the positive side is the fact that we are building a $9 million building in Vancouver, and that this will provide a substantial body of employment. I suggest it is not quite fair to attempt to emphasize the relatively few people who would be employed if we were to do certain other things.
Surely the main consideration is that we are building a very large building at a cost of over $9 million, and thereby providing a considerable amount of employment that otherwise would not be available if the building were not being erected. I can assure my hon. friend that we have gone to considerable extremes in other fields to ensure

that Canadian materials are used, and that the Canadian content of labour in this $9 million structure is kept at a very high level, indeed.

I should like to make a few remarks with respect to the discussion that took place before five o'clock regarding the use of Canadian products in public buildings. It is well known that the only real consumer of marble in Canada is the government itself. Most structures are built of cheaper products, stone, wood, brick and so on, especially concrete. With the government itself showing a bad example by importing marble from Italy, it kind of upsets the whole economy, particularly in my own part of Canada where we are very proud of the type of marble we can produce. In the interior of British Columbia, in the Kootenays and Okanagan valley, we can equal marble or any other stone produced in Italy or in any other country, and we are proud of that. At the present time we consider them depressed industries. Many of the quarries are closed down for lack of customers; many of the quarries have been pretty well closed down for the last ten years for that same reason; but recently the government itself was seeking a hard stone for an extension to the post office in Penticton, and they came to the conclusion that the stone that had already been in use in the old buildings for forty years or fifty years was the best stone that they had seen.
That is the impression given to me by the architect. This particular stone is produced in abundance. There is a vast deposit of it not far from Penticton. I understood at the time, two years ago, that the government were anxious to acquire the rights to that particular quarry. Whether they did so or not, I am not sure. But if they did, they
Supply-Public Works certainly have first-class stone equal to anything they can bring to this country from Italy.
On behalf of that depressed industry I would suggest that the government, before a contract is let for any more marble or any more hard stone from any other part of Canada, take steps to find out what we have in the province of British Columbia. If they do not wish to go to the expense of doing that, I may say that the provincial government already has all the information with regard to these various marbles and the hard rock that we have in such abundance. I would suggest to the minister that, in fairness to our province and before he places an order again for marble, he should take steps to find out whether a similar product is available in the Okanagan valley, the Kootenay valley or one of the other valleys in British Columbia.

The outstanding example in Canada today where local stone or Canadian stone has been used is this House of Commons. When you look at this building you see this beautiful stone which comes from Tyndall, Manitoba. That fact shows that the government is right on the job.

Architectural branch-
361.	Branch administration, $701,299.

This item covers branch administration of the architectural branch. Turning to the details on page 431 we find a list of people who are working in that branch. I take it from these figures that there are 28 architects, 23 engineers and 23 technical officers. Can the minister tell us whether or not those figures are correct?
I assume that my hon. friend has totalled the figures shown on page 431. I accept them as being correct. I have not totalled them myself.
Are these people all employed in Ottawa?
The answer to that question is yes.

What is the position of a member of this house if he wants to get from the architectural branch some information on plans and specifications and calling for tenders? The reason I raise this question is this. I am naturally interested in the Vancouver post office because I am a member from the city of Vancouver. Over a period of almost months now I have received communications from various unions asking about the type of architecture, about the construction, how much is granite, how many floors there are

Supply-Public Works and various other questions. I wanted to answer those questions. Several weeks ago I got in touch with the architectural branch of the Department of Public Works with regard to the post office. I asked if I could see the actual plans and specifications. That was weeks ago. I have never seen any plans or specifications to this date. Are they secret or what? When I, a member of the House of Commons, ask to see plans and specifications, why cannot I be allowed to see them?

There is no reason why not. A member of the House of Commons is quite entitled to see the plans and specifications of a building, once those plans and specifications are complete. Would the hon. member care to tell me-and perhaps he would care to do it privately-to whom it was he spoke? I should be glad to discuss the matter with him.
It was your chief architect.
The chief architect says that the plans and specifications have not been refused.
I have not got them.

I notice that there is a considerable increase in the number of personnel, from 128 to 158. I refer particularly to the point that I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was making. Quite a part of this increase in personnel is accounted for by an increase in the number of architects. Can the minister explain the reason for this increase amounting to over 20 per cent in the number of personnel required for branch administration in the architectural branch? Is there a great deal more building projected than was the case previously or is this chiefly for planning for what used to be called the shelf of public projects for the future? Or what is the general explanation?

The reason for the increase is to try to make our program of planning a little more current. We had a backlog because of the difficulty of obtaining architects and technical assistants. On more than one occasion my hon. friend has referred to the number of re votes. We are endeavouring to bring the program up to date, to get some of these revotes out of the estimates and to get on with the program of new work.
In other words, this increase is to put current work into operation, as you might say?
Yes; that is correct.
Rather than for future planning?
That is correct.

I am wondering whether it is the policy of the Department of Public Works to look after all the architectural functions for these various activities across the country or whether in some cases this work is handed out to private firms in the local area where the work is to be done?
There are many instances in which buildings are designed for the department by private architects. That is part of the department's policy.

Is it the policy in the public works department to do most of the architectural work or do they call in the private architects only when the departmental officials are not able to handle the quantity of work involved?

The general policy has been for the department to do the smaller buildings. Normally one design of building will serve the purpose of two or three different communities. It is standard practice to use that design to the extent that we can do so, having in mind the need to blend any building into the community. The larger buildings have almost invariably been designed by private architects because we regard that work as being beyond the capacity of our people to deal with, having in mind the heavy load of smaller work that is on them. When judged in the light of dollars and cents I would think the division would be just about even; I would think that about half of it would go to the private architects and that half of it would be done by our own people. It would be something of that order.

I have a question which I feel certain is in the minds of many members but perhaps they do not want to speak about it. What is in the mind of the minister with respect to the office accommodation of members of the House of Commons? In the majority of cases there are two members to an office at the present time, and I think that in all such instances they get along quite happily. But it does not make for efficiency in the work of members of the House of Commons.
Have you any particular members in mind?

Two members cannot be dictating to two stenographers at the same time without there being confusion. If one member has any visitors it disturbs the entire office. I think every member of the house who is in the position of occupying an office jointly with another member knows the problem. It is a very serious one, not only from the point of view of the efficiency of members of the House of Commons but also with respect to the impression that the general public gets from reading press comments about members not being in the house itself. It is my own personal experience that when two members occupy the same office they split up in shifts so that each can have the office to himself for a while in order to do his work and give his dictation. You cannot be both places at once. Every member knows that is the situation.
It is not fair to members of the House of Commons so far as their work is concerned and the reaction of the press is not fair in pointing out that often over half the members are not present in the house. We know that in the majority of cases they are in the building because when the division bell rings they take their seats in the house. I think one of the big problems is the matter of office accommodation for members. I believe that this vote is the proper place to raise the question, and I should like to ask the minister whether he has anything in mind that will bring about a better distribution of office space for members of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words under this item with respect to the rates of pay in the case of women cleaners, particularly those working in the federal buildings in the city of Winnipeg, who come under the direction of the Minister of Public Works. I am sure that he is well aware of what I am going to say because we have had a fair amount of correspondence concerning this matter. I only hope that by raising it on the floor of the house I might be more successful than I have been in taking the matter up with him by letter.
As the minister knows, when the five-day 40-hour week was instituted for civil servants generally-I refer to the time previous to the occasion when the five-day 40-hour week came into effect for postal workers-that had an effect on the wages received by the women cleaners in the city of Winnipeg which, from their standpoint, was most unfortunate, and I would say it was most unfair. Previously they had been working five and a half or six nights a week, and they were paid on an hourly rate. When the people working in the offices which were cleaned at night by these women went on the five-day week, naturally there was no point in having the cleaning women coming in on the sixth night and cleaning up the offices when those offices had not been occupied during the day. Therefore they, too, went on the five-day week.
Well, they did not mind going on the five-day week, but it was a rather tough blow for them to suffer an actual reduction in their weekly take-home pay as a result of that change. In the correspondence I have had with the minister he has suggested to me that I would not want people to be paid for work they were not doing. I suggest that that was a case of begging the question. The fact of the matter is that other employees of 83276-250
Supply-Public Works the government who went on the five-day 40-hour week did not suffer any loss in take-home pay. The purpose of the five-day 40-hour week was not to effect a reduction in pay but rather to improve the working conditions of the employee.
Generally speaking that change to the five-day 40-hour week for government employees was effected without any reduction in take-home pay. I have not the page references in Hansard before me at the moment, but I can say that during the course of this session I have inquired, through the medium of the order paper and by obtaining answers on the pages of Hansard, as to whether there are any other government employees in whose case the fact of going on the five-day 40-hour week resulted in a reduction in pay. The answers given to me suggest that this was the only group.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is quite unfair, and that something should be done about it. If the minister insists that these people are on prevailing rates and that that makes it impossible to prescribe that they shall now get per week what they got before, the problem could be solved by an increase in the hourly rate sufficient to bring these women up to the same amount of pay they were receiving before.
I know some people think of these women who do this work as though they were in parttime unemployment, or doing casual work. I do not presume to speak for what goes on in other cities, but I do know that these women who are working in the minister's department in Winnipeg are regular, year-round full-time employees. I know some of them personally who have been in this work for ten or fifteen years or more. So they are not to be thought of as casual or temporary employees, whatever their precise legal status may be. They have an arrangement for holidays; one they did not have some years ago, but an arrangement we were able to win for them. They pay unemployment insurance premiums, and they pay into one or other of the superannuation funds. To all intents and purposes they are just as permanent employees of the federal government as are any other employees.
I urge strongly upon the minister that the situation be reconsidered and that the necessary increase be made so that these women may continue to receive at least the same amount they were receiving before the five-day 40-hour week was instituted.
In the course of the correspondence the minister and I have had concerning this
3958	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works matter he has informed me that the usual survey has been made by the Department of Labour to determine whether or not the rates being paid to these people corresponded with the prevailing rates for comparable work in the same area. He has not been at liberty to indicate to me what is contained in the reports made to him by the Department of Labour, but he has suggested to me that these reports have indicated that his department was doing as well for these women as is the case with women doing comparable work in Winnipeg.
My information is not quite the same as that the minister appears to have received. I am told that women doing comparable work for the T. Eaton Company in Winnipeg are on a 40-hour week and that their rate of pay is seventy-five cents an hour or more. At the Hudson's Bay Company in Winnipeg the rate is exactly the same, seventy-five cents an hour; and, likewise, that is the rate for those working for the Canadian National Railways. Those who are cleaning in public buildings for the city of Winnipeg receive eighty-five cents an hour, and again they are on a basis of a 40-hour week. Women doing this kind of work for the Winnipeg public school board are paid on a monthly rate at the figure of $149 per month.
What about the provincial government?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sorry I do not have that information, but I have no objection to the suggestion by the Secretary of State that it should be taken into consideration. I hope, however, that he is not trying to show up the provincial government as being a poor employer.
Just a matter of curiosity.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
But as compared with these rates of seventy-five and eighty-five cents an hour, the rate paid to the women cleaners who work in Winnipeg for the Minister of Public Works is sixty-five cents an hour for a week of thirty-seven and one-half hours in the dominion public building, and sixty-five cents an hour for a thirty-hour week in the commercial building. There are still other buildings that come under the minister's supervision. There is the old post office building, and some others. While the hours per week may vary, I believe the sixty-five-cent rate carries right through.
I could continue the discussion on this point, but it seems to me I have made it clear. I do hope some favourable consideration will be given to increasing these rates so that these faithful employees of the government will not receive less than they were receiving before the five-day 40-hour week came into


effect. It seems to me two things are involved; One is the actual rate of pay and the other is that justice should be done.

Before recess, Mr. Chairman, may I say just a word. I have every sympathy for the point raised by the hon. member, who has been so interested in the pay received by these charwomen. The position is as he stated It. We have exchanged correspondence in which I informed him of the facts he has put before the committee. They are hourly rate employees. The Department of Labour conducted a survey at the time the hours were decreased to see whether a re-rating was justified. It is true there are private employers in the city of Winnipeg who pay more, but it is also true that the majority of private employers pay less.
After making a very exhaustive survey, the Department of Labour told the Department of Public Works that there was no ground for recommending an increase in the rate at the present time, but that the matter would be kept under review.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it government policy to match the minimum rate in the field?

It is to match the rate of good employers in the district.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing item 363. Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I have one or two words with the minister? At six o'clock we were discussing this question of the wages paid to women cleaners working for the Department of Public Works at Winnipeg. The minister said it was the policy of the government to match the best employers in the field.
No, I did not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What did the minister say?
I said "good employers".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: All right; I will accept that. He said it was the government's intention to match the good employers. Are not the good employers the ones who pay good wages?
What I said is a pretty good definition of the position. There is a difference between good, better and best, as my hon. friend well knows.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just a minute; that puts the government a long way down. Better is better than good and best is better still. So he puts himself in the third category. Seriously, I hope the minister will have this matter looked at again. If he cannot cut through the red tape but has to have another review made by the Department of Labour, I ask the minister to have such a review made in the light of the figures I put on the record this afternoon showing that other women in Winnipeg doing comparable work are getting better pay.

I have no objection to that, Mr. Chairman. I told my hon. friend that the matter was under constant review. We have every sympathy with the position of the charwomen in Winnipeg. The position was examined and it was then found that some employers were paying more to charwomen than our charwomen were receiving, but a great many of them were paying less, and on that basis the Department of Labour, which is the department that guides us in these matters, recommended that the rate be not changed at this time.
In reply to a question asked earlier by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra about the printing bureau I might say that the Department of Public Works has no request at the present time for electric fixtures but we have received a request for 400 fluorescent lights. These are being stocked to assure replacement of burnt-out tubes and to keep the replacement stocks in the building at a proper level. The replacement of tubes is high due to the long hours of operation at the bureau. The cost is approximately 69 cents each, so 400 comes to $276.
As to requisitions for work, a requisition was filed for resurfacing the press room floor and adjacent hall area with mastic in June, 1953, at a cost of $3,600, and that is the only requisition we have had.
An hon. member asked a question about foremen of char service and pointed out the fact that the list showed eight last year and this year there are eighteen. There are no new bodies, but ten positions of cleaner and helper have been reclassified by the civil service commission as foremen of char service.

I should like to return to
the subject of architects' service, for a moment. The minister has indicated that in some instances private architects are used. That being so, I should like to know the procedure involved in applying for work on government projects. The reason I ask is that a local firm has been in touch with 83276-250J

I do not think that is a proper function for a member of parliament to make overtures to the branch on behalf of architects.
The hon. member has done it. If it is not proper, then the hon. member has acted improperly.

I have had some correspondence on this matter because of the information that came to me, and I realized that under the administration of the minister this policy would not be carried out. I should like to have him indicate it so that it can be on the record and I can indicate to this firm that such is not the policy.

Hon. members, such as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, imply from time to time that Liberal members are the only ones who make requests of the minister. I might say that he is one who has made a request of me, in this case to have an architect, a friend of his, employed and I can see nothing very much wrong with that. But I do want to say that I receive at least as many requests from members of the opposition as I receive from Liberal members, and I see nothing wrong with that either. Hon. members are elected to represent their constituencies with respect to federal matters, and it is only right and proper that they should endeavour to do so.
As to the employment of architects, when outside architects are used in the design of public buildings, the fee is uniform so it is a question of choosing somebody who is competent. There are a great many competent architects in Canada, and I venture to say there are many competent architects in the constituencies of a good many hon. members on both sides of the house. When names are brought to my attention it is my practice to consult with the chief architect to get his opinion as to the competency of those people. I am not familiar with them all. I will be, I presume, as time goes on, familiar with more of them, but at the present time I must reply on the best advice I can get, and I endeavour to choose the architects that will deliver work which will be a credit to the Canadian people generally.

It is a brief question and has to do with the playing of the bells in the tower here. Who is responsible for deciding when the bells are played? What are the duties of the carillonneur apart from playing the bells? I notice that he draws a considerable salary. I think that is only fair. It is about half as much again as M.P.'s drew until recently. I am just wondering what the regulations are with regard to the matter, who is responsible for the programming, the hours and so forth.

The content of the program is his own. He is a very competent carillonneur. He reports to the deputy minister and confers on matters respecting administration generally; but normally he is left to his own devices to choose his programs and to choose the time of playing. It is pretty much the same time from year to year.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
Is there a set number of programs per week or per month, or what is the basis?
The program is set up at the first of each year and I think it is published and made available to the public in the form of a little booklet.

With regard to item 363, I am looking at page 438 and I see amounts for maintenance and operation of public buildings. I look at the details for New Brunswick and I see that the amount given there is about half of that for Nova Scotia. I thought perhaps that was just because there are not too many public buildings in New Brunswick. But in looking back three years I see that this amount was reduced to the present amount from an amount that was similar to that for Nova Scotia. There seems to be consistency in those amounts. I wonder whether the minister can explain why New Brunswick was cut down to such a small amount three years ago and has not been placed back in its former position.

We do not place moneys in the estimates unless we are going to spend the money. We do not place an amount in the estimates for maintenance and operation unless it is so required. My hon. friend will see that this year there is an increase over last year, the amount being $600,000 as against $560,000. That is just for necessary maintenance. Probably in the years to which he refers there was an especially big maintenance project at some particular place. I do not recall it but this is for actual costs of maintenance.

Would the reason that the New Brunswick figure is so low in relation to the Nova Scotia figure perhaps be that there was only half the number of public buildings in New Brunswick or is there any consistency there? The other amounts seem to be fairly well the same each year. Three years ago New Brunswick was well up over the mil-lion-dollar mark, where Nova Scotia is now. Then we were cut down to about $500,000. While there is an increase this year, I should like to have an explanation as to why the amount for New Brunswick is so low as compared with that for Nova Scotia. Is it because we do not have as many public buildings?
It is because the buildings in this current year do not need as much maintenance. That is the real reason.
I argue against that contention by saying that the amounts are fairly consistent each year in the case of the other provinces, as they have been for the last two or three years. There is no change.
I think my hon. friend should really be pleased that we are able to cut down the amount for maintenance and operation. Surely that is the type of economy he should be pleased about.
I am; in the other provinces.

necessary.

I should like to ask the minister when tenders will be called for the Pictou post office.
We plan to call for tenders for the post office in Pictou by June 15.

I might just ask the indulgence of the committee for a moment to take the minister on a Cook's tour of the constituency of Colchester-Hants, running from the Minas basin to Northumberland strait and review our public buildings. First, at Hantsport, Shubena-cadie and Stewiacke our buildings are in fairly good repair. I do not think the total for repairs of these buildings will be very much this year. Coming next to Windsor, I may say that last year we understood that the roof and the outside of that building which, by the way is very old-it was built in the early 1880's-was slated for some major repairs. Unfortunately they were not carried out. I should like to have the minister look into that matter to see if the repairs could be carried out this year. When he has looked over the other places in Nova Scotia, where new buildings are needed, I wish he would cast his eye there. I think it is nearly time that that building should be replaced.
I now come to Truro, the hub of Nova Scotia.
The what?

The hub of Nova Scotia. I am pleased to see that the plans which were brought into being a good many years ago at the time the reconstruction and rehabilitation committee was sitting building up the famous shelf of public works has now taken a little bit more definite shape, and that a lot has been purchased. I hope the construction of the building will be proceeded with without too much delay. I have already drawn to the attention of the minister the fact that the lot which the department has purchased is one of the finest lots in town, on the main street, one of the show places of Canada; and that the shade trees on the street make a wonderful arch. On that lot there are a number of nice trees. If I might just transpose my thoughts
Supply-Public Works for a minute, I might say to him that while speeches are made by fools like me, only God can make a tree. When they start to make their plans for that building I hope they will do everything possible to save as many of the trees as they can.
Now we shall go to the Northumberland strait and to the village of Tatamagouche. Back in 1940 the record will show that an amount was in the estimates for a public building at that point to house the post office. Plans were drawn, the contract was let and work was under way. The basement was dug. The forms were in. Some of the concrete was poured. Then owing to the stress of war, all work on public buildings of that nature was abandoned.
The work that was done was eventually demolished and the contractor settled with and on that vacant lot a temporary post office building was erected. The people of that flourishing community felt that when the contract had gone as far as that they would be sure to have a public building suitable for their needs in due course. However, so far there is nothing in the estimates for that and I would ask the minister to take this matter under advisement and discuss it with his colleague the Postmaster General. The former postmaster general must have approved this project otherwise the work would never have been started. If we could get that public building anywhere in this area it would certainly be a nice asset, and it is certainly much needed. There are five rural mail routes serving North Colchester based on this thriving village.
A few years ago it was my privilege to participate at the unveiling of a monument erected there by the national historical sites board to commemorate the naval battle of Tatamagouche bay. There is a nice monument there to commemorate this battle which took place during the early days of the country. It was not a very important battle but it was certainly considered important enough to erect a monument to commemorate it. I hope it will not be necessary for someone in the future to erect a monument to mark the spot where the public building was started but not finished.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer for a moment to the public building erected at Lockeport. It was my pleasure some few days ago to be in that town and to see the new public building there. It is a very well planned building and architecturally attractive. The exterior is of brick and Nova Scotia granite. Many of the citizens with whom I spoke were pleased to have such a fine building in their community. They felt it was

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask a few questions with reference to the New Brunswick vote. I note that there is $1,250,000 authorized for New Brunswick, but they are all revotes. Like the hon. member for Colchester-Hants and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, I would like to congratulate the minister on the fact that some buildings have been completed. But I would like to ask about the public building at Rothesay. I have brought this matter up on a number of occasions and the former minister of public works promised definitely both in 1952 and in 1953 that this building would be constructed. I do not think it is necessary to again point out the great necessity for this building. I do not suppose there is any place in Canada that needs a new post office more than Rothesay. The population there is increasing very rapidly, as I have pointed out before, and there are two private schools in that town. There is a large consolidated school and a new district high school. The population is increasing from about 100 to 150 every year and the building now in use there is an absolute disgrace as far as the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works are concerned. They have no facilities of any kind in this building. There are three or four employees and they have not even a washroom.
I understand there has been some difficulty over the selection of a site, but there is a good site near where the building used as a post office now stands and it could be purchased. I have been told, and the minister can correct me if I am wrong, that the reason this site has not been selected is because the owner of the land does not belong to the proper political persuasion.
Oh.

You may say "Oh" but you do not know my opponent in the last election. I would like to see some of the private correspondence with the department in that connection because I have every reason to believe that my opponent during the last election, and also one of the local candidates for another party, opposed the purchase of the site. I would like to have the minister's comments on this, and I would also like to

know if there is any possibility of this building being constructed in the immediate future.

It is a fact that the site has not yet been selected, and my hon. friend may be disappointed to know that to my knowledge I have received no communications of any kind from his opponent. I have one question for the minister. Can he tell me the story on the customs building in Saint John? I want to know what is going on, what are the details and what are the plans with respect to the future of that building.

Our proposal at Saint John is to carry out some quite extensive renovations, as I recall, to the existing building to try to keep it in as good shape as we can until such time as we can plan to build a new building there.

It is a very old building. People tell the story around Saint John about an official from Ottawa who came to visit the customs department there and who spent all his time in the office of one of the senior officials dodging the raindrops that were seeping through the roof and falling into pails
Supply-Public Works in this main office of the customs building. That will give you the story on the old building.
Can the minister tell us what the situation is with reference to the proposed customs and immigration building at St. Stephen and also the public building at Woodstock?

This item covers buildings in Ottawa. I would ask the minister to tell us whether anything has been done to carry out the recommendation made by the special committee on atomic energy last session. If the minister will recall, the committee was very much disappointed with the accommodation found for the work on radioactive minerals. We were shown through the basement of the museum. That was where much of this work was being carried on. I think every member of that committee felt that accommodation was not suitable for this work which is so important to Canada today. Nevertheless, in looking through the details of this vote I can find no provision for better quarters for carrying on this work. I ask the minister to explain whether I am wrong and, if so, to tell us just what accommodation is being provided for this work.

I should like to support the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The committee was privileged to visit the quarters supplied for this particular work at that time and they were very much disturbed about the accommodation. I know that it was the unanimous opinion of the committee that some improvement should be made. I believe it is most necessary and should receive every attention.

speechtext: I wish to thank the hon. gentlemen who are supporting us in this project. I think the minister will explain what is being done.

But no steps have been taken so far to acquire a site?

This afternoon I asked a question about the national library, and I think this is the appropriate item. Will the minister indicate what progress is being made on this project?
The architects, Messrs. Mathers and Haldenby, of Toronto, are working on the plans, and they have not yet quite completed their preliminary plans.
Will the national library have any connection at all with the parliamentary library?

No, it will be a separate operation.
IMr. Winters.]
How soon will the work on the parliamentary library be completed, and how much will it cost? Has the minister any information on that?

I am told, Mr. Chairman, it will be another two years before the job is completed. Hon. members who perhaps have looked in to see the work going on there will realize how complex it is. The whole building has had to be stripped right down to the masonry shell. It is turning out to be a much more expensive operation than could possibly have been foreseen. It will probably cost in excess of $2 million.
That is what I was told the other day, but I did not know whether or not that was right. It seems like a large sum. There is no doubt the building needs repair, but-
It is far more than a repair, it is a complete rebuilding.

A few weeks ago there was another fire in the library and the fire trucks came up here. What was the cause of that fire in the library? Was it because of a careless workman dropping a cigarette or what was it?

I do not think there was any carelessness, Mr. Chairman. There was simply a short circuit in the electrical wiring that ignited some of the woodwork in the dome. The fire was quickly brought under control and there was negligible damage.
Will the space in the library be enlarged or is it merely going to be fireproofed?
The capacity will be increased, and it will be fireproofed.
Does that mean the walls will be extended to increase the outside dimensions of the building or will there be an additional structure added?

No, there is going to be some further excavation, the basement is going to be deeper. There will be more accommodation there and the internal arrangements will be such that there will be more storage space for the books.
I see here there is an item of $900,000. Does that mean you think that amount will cover the cost for this year?
Yes, that is right.

Over half of this vote of $750,000 is for landscaping.

How large is the area to be landscaped?
I am told by the hon. member for Ottawa West it is about a mile square, but I have not that information.
What is the cost for the grading of this land? What is the total cost for grading?
The figure I gave includes the earth and rock grading and fill.
That is landscaping.

I rather think I am speaking on the right item. It appears on page 443, and apparently under that item you can deal with almost anything that is in or around Ottawa. Supply-Public Works
There are two additional gates on either side of the main gate. It seems to me that the space taken by these gates could easily be used to give additional width to the main gate. Mr. Chairman, Fort William is outside of Ottawa. We have been attempting to obtain a public building there, and the reason is that we are paying out over $30,000 in rent for dominion offices. We think it would be a saving to the dominion government to have all these offices in one place. A delegation came down here, and the minister treated them very well indeed, up to a point. It would seem that he is going to consider requests that are made. I headed different delegations to the former minister of public works, and in each and every case upon leaving him I thought that I would most certainly get what I had asked for. But as soon as the interview was over the former minister appeared to forget the interview completely. The result was that I never got anything.
I believe there is a request before the department now for a new post office at Exeter, which is very badly needed at that

Supply-Public Works point. There is an airport adjacent to Exeter, and in the last few years the post office has not had sufficient room in which to operate.
