We have not yet made that decision.

There are three items that interest me in this vote. First, there is the construction of the customs and immigration buildings at Boissevain, the addition and alteration to the public building at Brandon, and a similar estimate for the public building at Virden.
I rise at this time because each of these is a revote. In the cases of the first two, I believe they have been in the estimates for the last three or four years.


Dealing particularly with the customs port at Boissevain, I think the minister is aware that this matter is becoming increasingly urgent, because the customs port is located on highway No. 10 which today is becoming recognized as the main street of the Americas. It is a highway that runs right through from South America, through the international peace garden, the city of Brandon, and Riding Mountain national park. At the present time it continues as far as Flin Flon, Manitoba, which is an important mining section in the province. We would hope eventually, of course, as the north opens up that this highway of the Americas would extend right through to Churchill. I understand the great difficulty here is the matter of negotiation with American officials.
The hon. member is referring to Boissevain?
Yes.
The situation is that the plans are complete and they have gone to the secretary for advertising. Tenders will be called, to close on May 12, 1954. That will save the hon. member a speech.

I think we are seeing greatly improved efficiency in the department when we can get a response such as we have had just now concerning this item which, as I have indicated, has been on the books for the last three years.
Then, in regard to the addition and alterations to the post office at Brandon, I notice the amount this year is reduced from $150,000 to $50,000. I wonder if there is an explanation for that.

No; it just means that is probably all we will be able to spend this year. We expect to go out for tenders this year, but it will be late in the year and we do not expect we will be able to spend more than $50,000. However that does not mean anything in the final outcome.

It just indicates once again the new efficiency and the new look in the department. Then, finally, as the penultimate point, I would direct attention to the public building at Virden. I do not think there is any particular problem there, but I would point out that Virden is the oil centre in western Manitoba. At the present time it has all the appearances of a boom town with the result that post office facilities at the moment are greatly overcrowded. From what the minister has said in regard to the two other items I think we can safely conclude that this project, too, will receive the same expeditious attention.

There is one further matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention at this time. It is the need for a new federal building in the city of Brandon. I think the situation there is much the same as that in Fort William. At the present time, with the exception of the post office, federal offices are located in the old post office building. In that building are the employment offices, the unemployment insurance offices, and the headquarters for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The square footage available in the old post office building is only 1,720 square feet, which means that the insurance branch has overflowed into an upstairs office occupying a square footage of 1,100 square feet. My information is that these two branches alone require some 5,000 square feet of office space. The present accommodation available is just 2,820.
In addition to the lack of sufficient area, the fact that the two branches are dispersed at different parts of the city creates an administration problem of some significance. On top of that I understand that the C.M.H.C. is opening a new regional office to administer the new act, and will require further office space. Furthermore I believe the radio trouble unit is to be located in the city of Brandon, which will require further office facilities.
I will not labour the point other than to say that Brandon is the important urban area of western Manitoba, and is the second largest city in the province. As a matter of fact, it serves an area of 12,500 square miles, with a population of 105,000 people. Perhaps the minister will also be aware of the fact that there is an excellent piece of property lying between the old post office building and the new post office building which is just waiting to be used for a project of this kind. I bring this to the minister's attention. Some of these days he will be visiting the city to see for himself, and this is by way of preliminary information.

In respect of the new Winnipeg post office I am informed that the outside will be completed of brick from eastern Canada. Will the minister advise the committee why Manitoba Tyndall stone, such as has been used in other public buildings in greater Winnipeg, is not being used?

I am not in a position to say whether that is true or not, but I would be very surprised if that were true. We have appointed as architects the well-known firm of Green, Blankstein and Russell, and I shall be very greatly surprised if that were the case. However, it is something that I shall look into.

There is a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I am very happy to see the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in his seat because he will be interested in this matter. I had the honour to represent the former seat of Assiniboia from 1945 to 1949. During that period I had the good fortune to have the village of Kipling in my constituency, which, as anyone knows who knows the southeastern part of the province, is a very progressive town and in a prosperous farming district. I want to refer the minister to the vote on page 446 "Kipling-public building, revote $25,000". Last year there was a vote of $75,000 provided. I know we have finished the Criminal Code, but I do not recall anything in it covering political parties which go out and make false promises or commitments. I am happy to hear from the minister that the Department of Public Works of this government is going to get a new look. I am not going to make any insinuations that could not be backed up, but we have heard from various members that there could very well be political reasons why certain votes were not spent in certain buildings under construction.
With regard to the Kipling building, I rise primarily to emphasize the fact that was previously recognized by the Department of Public Works, namely, the real necessity for a new building in the village of Kipling. I had a great deal of difficulty getting answers to certain questions from the government.

Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend will allow me to interject I might be able to save him a speech. We propose to go out to tender on this building early in the summer, and if additional funds are required this year we shall ask for them in the supplementary estimates.

I am
very happy to get the information which the minister has just given. Nevertheless I do want to continue these few remarks to indicate to the minister that we are expecting him to go through with it. It is a fact that the department did have certain surveys in that village. I would suggest to him that when they undertake this building they work in close conjunction with the local authorities and the people concerned because it has been brought to my attention that if the site-I am not too sure of the site-selected is the one they intend to build on it may not be the proper one in the best interests of the village, unless more than one has been surveyed. I am suggesting that when you build you work in close co-operation with the local board of trade, the town council and others to make sure that it will be an asset to the town and will work in with town planning.
I am happy to hear what the minister has just said. I want to emphasize that you need a building there. There is a high revenue-
You are going to get it.

I am
going to make one other suggestion in view of the fact that the minister is so amiable tonight. It is that when they are giving consideration to this matter, they consider the R.C.M.P. detachment at that point. We have our R.C.M.P. stationed there. They have never had proper barracks. Would the minister now be kind enough to give me the assurance that when they are considering this building they will make it a joint building to house the R.C.M.P., which they can use as a barracks, as well as a post office for Kipling?
No; I will not give my hon. friend that assurance.

I would point out this consideration to the minister, and I am quite serious about it. If this department is not already giving consideration to this matter, it would be well to do so because I do not think we need two buildings in that village. One building properly constructed would be under your department. It would be the type of building which would be an asset to the town and would serve very well the two purposes. I am suggesting to the minister that he give consideration to that matter. Perhaps now that I have got this far, I might solicit the assistance of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to get the R.C.M.P. barracks in addition.

Since I have been given some publicity in this matter, just to set the record

straight I might say that Kipling is now in the constituency of Qu'Appelle, and that we have been in very close touch with the situation since August 11. We are working in very close harmony with the local people, with the Department of Justice which is in charge of the R.C.M.P., and with the minister in charge of the Department of Public Works. We are making quite definite progress. If the building costs more than $25,000, we are not going to leave a building there with the roof off. It is going to be completed and it will be a good one. When the necessity arises for the R.C.M.P. to put up a building we, together with the local organization, will be working together. That is outside of any political organization. I mean the town organization and so forth.

I hope the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is speaking with authority and for the government. Now that he says he has been on the job since August 11, there is another question I should like to ask him or the minister. It is in connection with some of the contracts which were let or given to the Lunam Construction Company. This matter was brought to my attention on a number of occasions. The committee will recall that the former member for Qu'Appelle, Mr. Dewar, resigned from the house just prior to the federal election. There were left certain contracts which were not fully paid to the subcontractors or there were certain moneys which should have gone to the subcontractors. It has been brought to my attention that certain truckers and other people who were working there and in the employ of the subcontractors were not paid. If the minister or the hon. member for Qu'Appelle would assure me that this matter has been cleaned up to the satisfaction of the subcontractors and their workers I should be very happy. It is a bad situation because some of these young men who were working there with their trucks never were paid, and they have either lost their trucks or have been put in an extremely awkward position. I should like the minister to make a statement with regard to that matter, or the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.

We are fully aware of the
situation and everything is being done to rectify the situation that we are aware of.

Since the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has taken the liberty to answer my question and not the minister, I should like to ask him this question. When he says that "everything is being done", does he mean payment in money or that it is certain underground things that we cannot see?

This, Mr. Chairman, is the hon. member who said he would make no insinuations. The speech was loaded with them.
The situation with respect to the subcontractors is that they have formed a committee to attempt to establish the validity and the quantum of the subcontracts. They have appointed a legal agent, a Mr. Pope, to act on their behalf. They have had meetings. From a conversation which I recently had with Mr. Pope, I understand that they are very close to agreement on how the remaining moneys should be apportioned and that they have agreement as to assignment from Mr. Lunam. We hope that before too long the situation will be satisfactorily disposed of in so far as we are able to apportion the remaining funds.

I must thank the minister for including an item for $110,000 for a public building at Kelvington. Earlier this afternoon I discussed Carrot River. I should like the minister at this point to give us some information as to how he decides where those public buildings are built. I know that the Post Office Department and the R.C.M.P. are all interested in getting quarters in the country. The minister has assured us that in the future these public buildings are not going to be built for political reasons. I think hon. members might be interested, however, in finding out how, for instance, Lemberg gets a new public building this year. I might mention that Lemberg is in Melville constituency.
When I was in parliament previously and referred matters of this type to the then postmaster general or to the then minister of public works, I was informed that until a centre had a post office revenue of $10,000, no consideration could be given to the erecting of a public building. I find that, for the last year for which information is available,. Lemberg had a revenue of $4,810. I find that, in the Melville constituency Lemberg, I tuna,, Langenburg, Fort Qu'Appelle and Balcarres, all with a revenue a good deal less than that of Carrot River, have public buildings. Saltcoats has been included. It probably is the centre in Melville which the Minister of Agriculture believes did not get the consideration that it deserved. But these six centres I mentioned in the Melville constituency either have public buildings or are in the process of receiving them.
As I said previously, there is not a centre in the Mackenzie constituency that has a public building. We had one at Fort Livingston seventy-five years ago but not
3970	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works now. But in the Mackenzie constituency Hudson Bay, Kelvington, Carrot River, Preeceville, Norquay, Porcupine Plain, Sturgis, and Buchanan all have greater revenue than has Lemberg. I would suggest that the post office revenue gives some indication as to the size of the community. I wish the minister would explain this matter. Perhaps he would rather leave it for the Postmaster General to discuss, although I am sure if we wait until the Postmaster General comes with his estimates, he will tell us that public works decides. 1 wish the minister would explain how it is that none of these centres in Mackenzie constituency with revenue in excess of Lemberg get a public building, while Lemberg, with a revenue of $4,810, gets a fine public building in the course of the last year. Can the minister tell us what the formula is? How is that Lemberg, for example, gets a public building and Carrot River does not?
I know that the hon. member does not have in mind that there is any political favouritism here.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The thought seems to be in the minister's mind.

The hon. member probably knows better than does anybody else that the constituency of Mackenzie was represented for the past four years in a distinguished manner by a prominent Liberal. If the hon. member is accusing the government of not doing anything for the constituency for the past four years, surely he cannot say that the grounds were political.
There are certain principles here which, I think, should be made clear. In the first place it is very rare for the Department of Public Works to build a building for itself. It will not build a building for its own purposes in Kelvington or Carrot River or the other places mentioned by my hon. friend. The buildings it does construct are erected only because some other government department requires the type of accommodation which can be had only by building.
The other point is that these departments look to the Department of Public Works to provide suitable accommodation. Suitable accommodation does not automatically mean that new accommodation must be built. The $10,000 division line of revenue is a guide. The Post Office Department does not like to have new buildings erected in centres where revenue is less than $10,000 per year. But that does not mean that a new building cannot be built in a centre smaller than that,


because if suitable existing accommodation cannot be found in a small centre then the only alternative is to build new accommodation. It also applies that there are centres where revenue is greater than $10,000 per year and where it is satisfactory to use existing accommodation rather than build new accommodation.
What a story.

It is a true story, my hon. friend may be surprised to know. It is a fact that the Department of Public Works and the other departments of government concerned use their best judgment to solve the problem in the public interest.

I wish to thank the minister for his statement and I accept it as a statement of policy. The problem that I have been discussing did not arise while the minister was in charge. However, I think it is unfortunate that in an election campaign a candidate gets up and states, "You cannot get anything because your member of parliament is not a supporter of the government". I believe it is important that these decisions be based on an established formula, regardless of the political views of the sitting member. I must say, however, that the minister has been very courteous in handling all my correspondence and I would like to say that I have never felt a problem has been rejected because of any political difference of opinion I might have had with the minister. I again must emphasize that it is unfortunate that during the election campaign it was suggested that because Mackenzie had been represented by a C.C.F. member for a number of years no public building had been built there. As regards Carrot River it should not be suggested that they cannot have a public building now because a Liberal member does not represent that constituency. I simply want the minister to assure us that during the next four years a decision against building a public building at Carrot River will not be based on the fact that the people there did not send a Liberal member to parliament at the last election.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to thank the minister for the fine work that has been done in erecting a splendid federal building in the city of Yorkton. In that regard, I would like to ask the minister when he expects the work to be completed and whether he can give us some idea of the total cost? The building was very much needed and I can assure the minister that it is very much appreciated by the people of that city and the surrounding district. They will be very interested in finding out when it will be ready to be occupied.

The people are particularly anxious to know the completion date, because they were told during the election that the best thing to do was to vote Liberal in order to get the building finished. I would like to have the minister's comments on that.

The building at Yorkton is under contract to W. C. Wells Construction Company and the amount involved is $766,047. About 70 per cent of the building has been finished and the job should be completed within the next three months.
There was a revote on the first estimate and I believe the figure then was $225,000. The second year there was a revote of $350,000, and this year it was $450,000. What is the total figure?
And you expect to have it finished this year?
Yes.

With regard to the other post offices I might say, in line with what the minister said tonight, that there are one or two places in my constituency where accommodation for post offices at the present time is very poor. I refer to the village of Theodore and the village of Raymore. As regards the village of Kelliher, they too, have a fairly large revenue, and although they have fair accommodation it is not nearly as good as in the neighbouring village of Ituna, or the town of Lemberg, which happens to be in the constituency of Melville. The revenue at the village of Kelliher is higher than at Ituna and considerably higher than at Lemberg. However, I hope the minister keeps these things in mind and remembers the very poor accommodation which they have at Theodore and Raymore.

Mr. Chairman, I notice in the details there is an item for accommodation for government services in Calgary on revotes which amounts to $150,000. I would also like to know where that building is to be erected in Calgary and what size it is to be.

This amount is required toward the construction of a public building in Calgary to provide improved accommodation for the Department of Veterans Affairs and other government services. I am not
Supply-Public Works yet in a position to tell my hon. friend how large the building will be. We have not progressed far enough with the planning to know the answer to that question.
I take it from the minister's remarks that this is not to be the total cost of the building and that this is merely the preliminary vote in order to get it started. Is that the situation?
Yes, that is correct.

And I take it also from what the minister said that this is the same building for which votes were passed, I believe, in 1947-48 and in 1948-49 in regard to the veterans' affairs building. The Department of Veterans Affairs has requested us to erect a new building on a site which is owned by them opposite the Colonel Belcher hospital. Mr. Chairman, I wish to say something about this item before it is passed. There has been some comment this evening about political favouritism in the Department of Public Works. I do not agree with that, Mr. Chairman, and for this reason: during the past 20 years the town of Banff has been represented by a Liberal and a Conservative. Very little has been done in the town of Banff. It is the most outstanding summer resort on the North American continent-
Oh, oh.

-and it deserves some consideration. I have just been reminded that it is now being represented by myself, a Social Crediter, and that may be the reason why it is being given some consideration by the Department of Public Works. Certainly that could not be considered as being political favouritism. I notice in the estimates that the department is going to spend $280,000 for a new public building in Banff. I imagine that sum will be to get it started. I do not suppose that will be the amount which will be required to complete the building. It should make a very handsome building in Banff national park. The provincial government also has its eye on Banff since the last election, and they are now erecting a building which will cost more than $250,000 to house one of the most modern telephone services in Canada.

Supply-Public Works
These two buildings are going to be a great asset to the town of Banff, and well they should because Banff attracts more tourists than any other spot in Canada. There is a problem in connection with the building to be erected by the Department of Public Works that I want to bring to the minister's attention. I have already discussed the matter with the Department of National Revenue. I should like to know whether provision is made in the plans for quarters for customs officers. I am informed, and I think accurately, that there is a considerable amount of business for such an office.
The answer to that is yes.

I am very glad to hear that. A customs officer is stationed at the Banff Springs hotel during the summer season. I am informed by one business concern in Banff that last year they paid over $7,000 in duties in a period of eight months. That is only one firm, so there must be sufficient business to warrant the opening of a customs office. I am very pleased to hear the minister say that provision is being made for that type of service. Can the minister tell the house what progress has been made? Has the site been selected?
As my hon. friend probably knows, the building will be constructed on a crown site, so we own the site now.
You have the site?
We have the site.
Where is it?
It is at the corner of Bear and Buffalo streets.
Is provision also being made in that building for the R.C.M.P.?
No.
I was informed that it would be possible for the R.C.M.P. to be housed in the new building and that the building which they now occupy would be used for other services. Is that correct?
That is not correct. We do not propose to house them in this new building.
What will be the over-all cost of the building when it is completed?
It is estimated that it will be around $300,000.
Can the minister say when construction will be started?
We hope to call for tenders by the 15th of May.
How long do you think it will take to complete construction?
I think it could be done within a year and a half.
I want to thank the minister for giving this matter the consideration that it deserves.

I was very glad to see that the item for the public building at Stettler had been increased from $75,000 to $125,000. I wonder whether the minister can say what progress is being made with the erection of the building and just what purpose it will serve. I understand it will house the new post office, but what other services will it provide accommodation for?
Post office and veterans affairs.
Can you say what progress is being made?
The contractor is J. C. Had-dow. The amount is $222,000. The contract was awarded in September and the building is 25 per cent completed.

I was wondering where the money had gone that was in last year's estimates for a public building at Wetaskiwin, and now I think I know. It went to Stettler. In all seriousness, I do want to voice the protests of the people of the city of Wetaskiwin against the government's action in dropping all mention of a public building in Wetaskiwin from the estimates this year. The need for this building has been recognized for some time. As a matter of fact, two years ago the sum of $50,000 was included in the estimates, and I believe that was intended for an extension to the existing building. Apparently it was recognized last year that an extension was not sufficient, and the sum of $75,000 was put in the main estimates toward the construction of a new building. Suddenly this year it is dropped.
Surely the priority has not disappeared so quickly. Conditions in that post office are intolerable not only for the public but also for the employees. The employees are working in cramped quarters and do not have proper facilities. People are forced to line up for their mail. When I was home at Christmastime people were standing in line an hour or more in order to get their mail. The employees could not get the mail sorted on time and people were delayed. Letters were coming in late and things were in a general uproar.

Since the item was first put in the estimates two years ago the situation in Wetaskiwin has worsened tremendously. The population of the city has increased to the extent where it has overloaded the facilities of the post office. Business has also increased to a very great extent. The Wetaskiwin area now has five full oilfields completely circling the city and it serves at least a part of one other field. That makes a total of six oilfields, and all the oil companies have their offices there. The oil supply companies have offices there. The drilling equipment and equipment repair companies also have offices in the city. These businesses are all forced to use the facilities of the post office in Wetaskiwin. As I said a moment ago, the situation there is terrible. The need for a new post office was recognized at least two years ago by the department.
The estimates were passed by the House of Commons. Surely, the minister cannot say that with the expansion of business within that city there is no longer any priority for a new building there. It would appear to me that if there were a need two years ago there is a double need for a new building now. I want to repeat that I protest most strongly the withdrawal of this item from the estimates. I should like an explanation from the minister as to why this item was dropped from the estimates when the need is so obvious.

The explanation is short, Mr. Chairman. A site had not yet been acquired, and when we compiled the estimates and the treasury board found we were not in a position to go ahead with the building because we did not have a site, they asked us to drop the item from the estimates this year so the equivalent amount of money could be used somewhere else where construction could be put in place.
I would presume, then, that a site will be obtained this summer, or at least negotiations for a site undertaken, so a start can be made on the building early next year.

When I spoke on March 12 when the first item of this department was before us, I made a reference to five projects in Alberta which had been dropped, we hoped only temporarily. When the minister replied it happened that I was called out of the house, but from what he said I am rather inclined to believe he may have misunderstood me. He referred to the $3,600,000 appropriated for the ensuing fiscal year, which represented an increase of $1,299,999 and said this would indicate there was no
Supply-Public Works attempt whatever to discriminate on any grounds that may possibly have been in the mind of the hon. member.
Upon reflection I believe the minister will agree that I did not charge discrimination at all. 1 asserted that there were other people who support the minister's party who were charging discrimination by inference, if not directly, inasmuch as they asserted that if an opposition member were representing the constituency that would be the best guarantee we would not secure a public building. I challenged that statement myself and said that, so far as I could ascertain during my fourteen years here, the policy was not one of discrimination. I would not want him to think for a moment that, so far as Alberta was concerned, I thought there was a suggestion of discrimination.
My entire comment was to the effect that, inasmuch as parliament last May had given its approval to the five projects, including the one in my own town of Innisfail, I trusted the minister would keep these matters to the fore and would agree to go through with these projects. After all, as I emphasized then and as I emphasize now, the need was recognized. The projects were given a high priority rating and everyone had cause to believe the projects would be undertaken. I was pleased to note that on March 12 the minister made it clear the projects had not been abandoned. I had used that term, and I am pleased to know that. I hope these projects have not been taken away completely, and that in another year the minister will find it possible to proceed with those projects to which I referred on March 12.
As I say, my only purpose tonight is to stress the fact that at no place in my remarks, either on March 11 or 12, did I charge discrimination against my constituency or against Alberta.

I am pleased to see the department has allocated some funds for the erection of public buildings in the city of Edmonton. I have no quarrel with where that money is to be spent because all parts of Edmonton are important to me. Naturally, I am sorry that not one cent is to be allocated to Edmonton East, which is one of the oldest parts of Edmonton and perhaps the most important. I am curious to know, and I would appreciate if the minister would be kind enough to explain, why the proposed public building in Edmonton, which was originally designed for Edmonton East, was switched to Edmonton West. What were the

Supply-Public Works reasons for that switch, and were any political motives responsible for the change?
I do not know of any switch being made since I have been in this department, Mr. Chairman. No switch was made, and therefore the second part of the question does not need an answer.
The proposed public building now being built in Edmonton West was originally to be built in Edmonton East; that was the understanding of the people of Edmonton.
That was all before my time; I do not recall it.
That may be, but I was anxious to know the reason for the switch.
I do not know.

Just before the item
carries, I desire to thank the minister and his department, on behalf of the Lethbridge federal riding, for the construction of three fine public buildings in the Lethbridge riding, namely Taber, Carway and Lethbridge. The building in Carway is particularly important because of the fact it is a rather vital port of entry to the Waterton Lakes park. It is entirely fitting that there should be a respectable public building there because of the great number of tourists going through the port of entry yearly.

Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings-
374.	British Columbia, $4,450,000.

I rise to make a few comments on this item with a particularly clear conscience because I represent the constituents who are most reasonable in their requests. They never ask for anything unless it is urgently required, after due consideration, and so on. I know the minister's officials, and I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that for some ten years the present public building in Trail has been inadequate, both as to size, as to facilities and as to conveniences. The greatest objection to the present building is the fact that the staff working in the basement often works under insanitary conditions. Whenever there is high water or a storm, the sewage backs up into the basement and the postmen find it very difficult to continue sorting letters because of the odours that are caused by this sewage.


I realize the department has had rather unusual difficulty in choosing a site because it has not been an easy matter to find a suitable site in the city of Trail for the proposed building. The local organizations and the local people are looking forward now to the commencement of this proposed building. I should like the minister to inform me just how far plans have proceeded and when we can expect tenders to be called. I should like to ask the minister about two other projects to save him rising on three occasions, because I believe in the conservation of the minister's energy.
I notice a vote of $100,000 for the city of Nelson. There, again, there has been some delay owing to the willingness of the department to consider a change in site to accommodate the city council. That is very much appreciated. However, they are greatly concerned about the commencement of work on the building. When can we expect tenders to be called for the building in Nelson?
Then I notice a public building for Castle-gar, in the amount of $50,000, and I am pleased indeed to see this amount set out in the estimates. Castlegar is a rapidly growing *community, possibly the most rapidly growing, with the exception of one in the constituency of the deputy chairman. I think it is a very good thing to consider placing a public building there. What are the plans in connection with that building, and when can construction be expected?

First of all, we are planning a building for Castlegar. The site has been acquired. Sketches have not yet been started, but we hope that we will be able to go out to tender on the building before the end of this fiscal year, that is, before the end of March 1955.
In Nelson we are going to build the building on a crown site. Sketches have been approved, and we hope we will be able to go out to tender within a month.
In Trail we plan to build on a crown site. Revised sketches are being prepared, and we hope to call tenders late this year.

I notice there are two amounts for Vancouver, in connection with item 374. Perhaps I should preface any question I have to ask by saying that, so far as we know, we have no political troubles, as they have adjacent to Melville in the province of Saskatchewan. However we have

not yet heard from the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. In any event I do not expect problems of that kind to develop under the administration of the Minister of Public Works.
The first item for Vancouver is a customs building with a vote of $1,200,000, and the second is a post office building with a vote of $2 million, including a revote of $780,000. Will the vote in the estimates now for the customs building be sufficient to complete it?
The amount of the contract for the customs building at Vancouver is $2,854,589. So the amount in the estimates will need to be supplemented by about $850,000.
Has the contract been let for the post office? I believe tenders have been called.

Tenders have been called, but the contract has not yet been let. We know what the amounts of the tenders were, but they are still in process of being scrutinized. The contract has not yet been awarded.

I do not suppose the
minister can say when it is expected work on the post office building will be begun. I might add that a very substantial fence was built around the lot on which the post office is to be built. There was some fear expressed through notices in the press, and by certain people in Vancouver, that the fence was of such a substantial type that it meant that the post office would not be built for a long time. I hope the minister will be able to reassure the people of Vancouver that the post office will be proceeded with as soon as the tenders can be properly analysed.

The recommendation to
treasury board in favour of the lowest tender is in the course of preparation now. The submission will go forward presently, and I would imagine that the contractor would be able to start there within the next month, at any rate.

We are very appreciative in the Fraser valley of the fact that a new immigration and customs building is being constructed at Huntingdon, and also for the fact that there is a revote in the amount of $70,000 for the public building at Mission City. Will the minister state what stage the plans have reached in connection with the Mission City post office?
Supply-Public Works

At Huntingdon the building is fifty per cent completed. Perhaps the hon. member has seen the building in progress. At Mission City we have a crown site. Sketch and plans have been prepared but detailed plans are not yet ready. We hope however that within the course of the next two months we will be able to call tenders for it.
Mr. Chairman, I believe I would require about five minutes for what I have to say. Perhaps we should call it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Well, the committee has not done badly this afternoon. Perhaps it would be well to call it ten o'clock, report the resolutions and ask leave to sit again.
Before that is done, I believe the minister was going to give an answer to me.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked me to give some information as to what was included in the general item found at page 438, in the amount of $809,000. That amount is principally for purchasing lock boxes, and furniture in bulk for future distribution, for travelling expenses not especially allotted, and for moving government departments within the various provinces.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
